Emotion Regulation in Pain
Abstract
1

##### ABSTRACT

Chronic pain and emotional problems are common, often co-occur, and result in substantial suffering and social costs. Cognitive Behavioral Ther-apy (CBT) is a family of treatments that have been extensively studied and has empirical support for its effectiveness in treating both conditions. How-ever, CBT show small benefits for patients with comorbid pain and emo-tional disorders, and treatments are mostly adapted for one condition or the other. Hence, there is a need for transdiagnostic interventions, target-ing both problematic pain behaviors and emotional components. In this thesis, I present results from three experimental studies investigating pos-sibilities to refine and enhance CBT for chronic pain patients with emo-tional distress by using emotion regulation strategies and skills training from mindfulness-based interventions.
In Study I the aim was to evaluate the efficacy of a tailored transdiag-nostic hybrid treatment, integrating basic CBT principles with strategies from Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), an acceptance and mindfulness-based approach developed for individuals with difficulties regulating emo-tional responses. The hybrid treatment was compared in a randomised con-trolled trial to an internet-delivered active control condition (iCBT). Intent-to-treat analyses showed that the hybrid treatment had positive long-term effects 9 months after treatment on outcomes such as pain interference and symptoms of depression compared to the control condition. We concluded that the hybrid treatment may be considered an acceptable, credible, and efficacious treatment approach.
In Study II the aim was to investigate the importance of hypothesized treatment processes of the hybrid treatment, specifically pain-related
dysregulation (catastrophizing, fear-avoidance, and non-acceptance of pain), and general emotion dysregulation (difficulties to regulate a wider range of emotional responses). Mediation analysis within the framework of structural equation modelling (SEM), using the full intention-to-treat sam-ple, showed that decreased pain-related dysregulation mediated the effects of the hybrid treatment on both pain interference and symptoms of depres-sion. Furthermore, indirect effects through pain-related dysregulation were more evident for participants scoring higher on this variable at base-line. In addition, decreased general emotion dysregulation mediated effects on symptoms of depression. We concluded that these findings provided further support for the conceptual principles of the hybrid treatment.
Emotion Regulation in Pain
2
The aim of Study III was to investigate the effects of components of mindfulness-based interventions, specifically looking at the importance of attentional focus during mindfulness exercises on experiences of experi-mentally induced pain using the Cold Pressor Test (CPT). In a mixed ex-perimental design, healthy participants were randomly assigned to brief mindfulness exercises with internal focus (body scan), external focus
(mindful listening), or a control group using spontaneous coping. Com-pared to spontaneous coping the mindfulness exercises had positive effects on pain tolerance, pain threshold, pain unpleasantness, frequency of nega-tive thoughts, and belief in thought content during the CPT. While our re-sults showed that changes in attentional focus were consistent with the ex-perimental manipulation, no significant differences were found between internal and external focus on any outcome measure. We concluded that the results did not support the notion that attentional focus would be es-sential for benefits of mindfulness, and that exercises with both external and internal focus could be beneficial when coping with pain.
In conclusion, the results from these studies support integrating basic CBT principles with emotion regulation strategies and skills training from mindfulness-based approaches to enhance treatments for patients with chronic pain and emotional distress. In addition, our findings provide some insights for future research regarding the importance of targeting pain-re-lated dysregulation, and the possibilities of using mindfulness exercises with different attentional focus.

##### SVENSK SAMMANFATTNING

Många personer med långvarig smärta beskriver även svårigheter att hantera känslor. Vid både smärta, ångest och nedstämdhet är det vanligt förekommande med orostankar, ältande och svårigheter att engagera sig i meningsfulla aktiviteter. Kognitiv beteendeterapi (KBT) innehåller ett fler-tal insatser inriktade mot förändrade aktivitetsmönster samt hantering av tankar och känslor. Dessa behandlingsmål kan beskrivas som transdia-gnostiska då de kan påverka livskvalitet och mående vid ett flertal olika di-agnoser. KBT anses ha vetenskapligt stöd vid såväl långvarig smärta som nedstämdhet och ångestproblematik. De flesta behandlingsstudier gäl-lande KBT vid långvarig smärta fokuserar dock främst på smärthantering, vilket tycks vara mindre effektivt vid samsjuklighet med depression eller ångest. Avhandlingen består av tre delarbeten som undersöker möjligheter att utveckla och förbättra KBT-behandlingar för patienter med långvarig smärta och emotionell problematik genom att använda känslohanterings-strategier och färdighetsträning från mindfulnessbaserade interventioner.
Syftet med det första delarbetet var att utvärdera effekterna av en transdiagnostisk ”hybridbehandling” som integrerar grundläggande KBT-principer med färdighetsträning i känslohantering från dialektisk beteen-deterapi (DBT). Hybridbehandlingen jämfördes i en randomiserad kon-trollerad multicenterstudie med en aktiv kontrollgrupp som fick internet-baserad KBT (iKBT). 115 patienter med långvarig smärta och samtidig emotionell problematik slumpades till någon av de två behandlingarna. Samtliga deltagare fyllde i formulär avseende psykiskt mående, smärta, smärthantering och aktivitetsförmåga innan och efter behandling, samt vid uppföljning nio månader efter avslutad behandling. De som fått hybridbe-handlingen angav efter insatserna en större minskning av oro för smärta, samt en ökad förmåga att genomföra aktiviteter trots smärta. Vid uppfölj-ning angav de som fått hybridbehandlingen fortfarande en ökad förmåga att genomföra aktiviteter, samt minskad nedstämdhet jämfört med iKBT. Totalt uppgav 72% av de som fått hybridbehandlingen, och 56% av de som fått iKBT, tillförlitliga förbättringar inom något av områdena; smärta, smärthantering, aktivitetsförmåga, ångest eller nedstämdhet.
Syftet med det andra delarbetet var att undersöka betydelsen av för-bättrad känslohantering för utfallet av hybridbehandlingen. Analyserna vi-sade att deltagare i hybridbehandlingen upplevde större förbättringar av-seende förmågan att hantera känslor efter avslutad behandling än delta-gare som fick iKBT. Vi fann även att dessa förbättringar hade ett tydligt samband med minskad nedstämdhet, samt ökad förmåga att genomföra
Emotion Regulation in Pain
4
aktiviteter trots smärta vid uppföljning efter nio månader. Vidare analys visade även att effekterna var mer uttalade för deltagare som skattade större svårigheter att hantera känslor relaterade till smärta före behand-ling.
Syftet med det tredje delarbetet var att undersöka betydelsen av upp-märksamhetsfokus i mindfulnessbaserade interventioner vid smärthante-ring. 204 friska deltagare randomiserades till en kortare mindfulnessöv-ning med inåtriktat fokus (kroppsscanning), utåtriktat fokus (medvetet lyssnande), eller en kontrollbetingelse. Samtliga deltagare utförde före och efter betingelsen ett kallvattentest där de ombads att hålla en hand i iskallt vatten så länge det upplevdes uthärdligt. Vi undersökte sedan förändrad smärttröskel, smärtintensitet, smärttolerans, samt smärtrelaterat obehag och ångest. Resultaten visade att båda mindfulnessövningarna hade posi-tiva effekter på smärttolerans, smärttröskel och upplevt obehag under kall-vattentestet jämfört med kontrollbetingelsen. Även om resultaten visade att deltagarna hade olika uppmärksamhetsfokus efter övningarna, hittade vi inga signifikanta skillnader mellan inåtriktat och utåtriktat fokus på nå-got av utfallsmåtten.
Vi kunde utifrån dessa studier dra slutsatsen att förbättrad känslohan-tering kan vara ett relevant behandlingsmål för patienter med långvarig smärta och emotionell problematik, samt att strategier och övningar med olika uppmärksamhetsfokus från mindfulnessbaserade interventioner kan vara användbara för att arbeta med denna målsättning. Hybridbehand-lingen tycks vara en effektiv metod som kan förbättra psykiskt mående och funktion i denna patientgrupp genom ökad förmåga till känslohantering.

##### INTRODUCTION

Chronic Pain and Emotional Distress
Chronic Pain
According to the definition by the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP), pain is an “unpleasant sensory and emotional expe-
rience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or poten-tial tissue damage” (Raja et al., 2020). This definition is universally appli-cable to all pain conditions, irrespective of their duration or underlying pathophysiology. In the article by Raja et al. (2020), proposing this defini-tion, it is emphasized that pain is a personal experience often unequal to the physiological process of nociception since it is also influenced by other factors.
Many individuals describe reoccurring or long-lasting pain for more than 3-6 months, hereby referred to as chronic pain. The prevalence esti-mates of chronic pain vary widely between studies. In Sweden it is esti-mated that around 20% of the population experience moderate to severe chronic pain, and 25% of these individuals report that pain have an impact on their ability to work (Breivik et al., 2006; Harker et al., 2012). According to the widely accepted biopsychosocial model, the experience and conse-quences of chronic pain arise from complex interactions among various bi-ological, psychological, and social factors. These factors (e.g., pain sensa-tions, stress responses, expectations, and social support), mutually influ-ence each other, and the importance of each factor can vary between indi-viduals and among individuals over time (Gatchel et al., 2007).
Pain and Emotional Distress
Emotional distress is a broad term, often used to describe a state of emotional discomfort that can manifest in various contexts, including psy-chiatric disorders and chronic illnesses (Bragard et al., 2017; Daly & Mac-chia, 2023; Gratz & Tull, 2010; Lavender et al., 2011; Lumley et al., 2008; Svanberg et al., 2017).
Since the criteria for most psychiatric disorders include the presence of distressing emotional experiences (Sheehan et al., 1998), it can be seen as an inherent aspect of these conditions. While not all chronic pain patients consistently report elevated levels of emotional distress, even among those seeking treatment (Svanberg et al., 2017), negative emotional experiences are also common among individuals suffering from chronic pain (Lumley et al., 2011). Moreover, according to a recent review by Velly & Mohit
Emotion Regulation in Pain
12
(2018), several studies have demonstrated that individuals with chronic pain are more likely to suffer from depression and anxiety.
Research in the fields of neurobiology, psychology and sociology has investigated potential connections between emotions and pain (Keefe et al., 2001; Lumley et al., 2011), and some authors have suggested that emo-tional distress and psychiatric disorders could precede and increase the risk of chronic pain. However, most studies supporting these hypotheses are cross-sectional or retrospective, and the relationship may both be bi-direc-tional and influenced by a third factor (Lumley et al., 2011; Velly & Mohit, 2018). For example, major depression and chronic pain share several as-pects, such as worry and emotion dysregulation, as well as difficulties ini-tiating behaviors, and lack of positive and meaningful experiences (Linton & Bergbom, 2011). Regardless of how we look at the association between them, chronic pain and psychiatric disorders are common, often co-occur, and result in substantial suffering, marginalization, and social costs (Bo-ersma & Linton, 2005; The Swedish Social Insurance Agency, 2023; Sulli-van et al., 2006; Velly & Mohit, 2018). This underscores the necessity to develop effective interventions for patients experiencing these symptoms.
Available Treatments Numerous psychological treatment approaches have been developed to
address chronic pain (Williams et al., 2020), and the multitude of options to consider becomes even more extensive when considering treatments from other disciplines. Interdisciplinary interventions are often recom-mended when it is necessary to address both physical, medical, social, and psychological factors (Gerdle et al., 2022). While these interventions can yield positive results, they can be costly and time consuming since they en-compass several professionals working together in an integrated manner (Ringqvist et al., 2019; Dragioti et al., 2019). To help patients with pain and emotional distress, interdisciplinary treatments often include approaches from cognitive and behavioral therapies (Gerdle et al., 2022). To sharpen the scope of this thesis, I will hereby focus on these interventions.
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is a family of treatments that have been extensively studied, with empirical support for its effectiveness in treating chronic pain (Eccleston et al., 2013), and psychiatric disorders (Hofmann et al., 2012). Several treatment packages are often included un-der this label, including exposure in vivo, operant behavioral therapy, and acceptance and mindfulness-based interventions (Turk et al., 2008; Wil-liams et al., 2020).
Introduction
13
CBT treatment packages for chronic pain typically involve a combina-tion of interventions including a) exposure and operant interventions to decrease avoidance and increase adaptive behaviors and activities; b) re-laxation training, mindfulness exercises, acceptance or hypnosis exercises targeting experiential avoidance, tension and hypervigilance; and c) pain education or exercises targeting misdirected or ineffective problem-solv-ing, negative thinking, catastrophizing or dysfunctional rule-governed be-havior (Lamb et al., 2010; Linton & Shaw, 2011; van Koulil et al., 2010; Wetherell et al., 2011).
A Cry for Transdiagnostic Interventions
Despite numerous efforts to compare outcomes of different CBT treat-ments for chronic pain, many patients still show no benefits, and average effect sizes are small to modest, suggesting that further improvements are needed (Morley et al., 2013). CBT is often considered a family of therapies with similar origins, however important differences regarding treatment aims and content should be considered when analysing outcomes, and these are often overlooked in reviews (Eccleston et al., 2013). Moreover, several trials of CBT treatments for chronic pain patients report ceiling ef-fects on outcomes such as symptoms of depression, mostly due to including non-depressed or mildly depressed patients (Greco et al., 2004; Kaapa et al., 2006; Mangels et al., 2009). In contrast, there is also evidence to sug-gest that a high levels of catastrophizing and distress can predict poor treat-ment outcomes, and that existing treatments may be less effective for pa-tients with comorbid chronic pain and emotional problems (Bergbom et al., 2011; Flink et al., 2012, 2014; Morley et al., 2008). I would argue that this is unsurprising since the focus in pain rehabilitation is pain management, and interventions targeting emotional problems are seldom as exhaustive or extensive as recommended in CBT for psychiatric comorbidities (Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014; Barlow, 2014; Turk & Gatchel, 2002).
Targeting transdiagnostic processes, underlying both pain and emo-tional problems, has been suggested as a strategy to improve treatment out-comes (Linton, 2010; Linton & Bergbom, 2011). Indeed, CBT often target aspects of affect, behavior, and cognition that are not necessarily specific to diagnoses, and in recent years there has been an increased interest in pro-cess-based (Hofmann & Hayes, 2019) and other transdiagnostic ap-proaches (Schaeuffele et al., 2021). Several studies have examined the com-mon factors of treatments, finding small to large effects of targeting cogni-tive and behavioral processes, as well as small to medium effects of other factors such as therapeutic alliance and homework assignments (Kazantzis et al., 2018). A recent review of mediating processes in CBT for chronic pain by Murillo et al. (2022), concluded that reductions in pain catastrophizing, pain-related avoidance, as well as increased self-efficacy and acceptance
Emotion Regulation in Pain
14
seem to mediate effects on disability. While the authors emphasize that more studies are needed to confirm these findings, the results indicate that multiple factors often targeted in CBT treatments for emotional disorders, are equally relevant to target among individuals with chronic pain. How-ever, before I go further into detail on transdiagnostic treatments, I will briefly describe the basic principles and theoretical framework of CBT.
Basic principles of CBT CBT has evolved from two distinct approaches: behaviorism, founded by B.F. Skinner, and cognitive therapy, founded by Aaron Beck. Modern CBT is based on behavioral analysis, which has strong foundations in ex-perimental research and learning theory (Hofmann & Asmundson, 2017; Treanor et al., 2015). Over time, CBT has been enriched by theories about thoughts and cognition that vary depending on the philosophical approach and history of the specific school. For example, traditional cognitive ther-apy focuses on changing negative thought patterns (Beck, 1976), while functional contextualism and relational frame theory emphasize the im-portance of context in shaping behaviors (Hayes et al., 2006). Additionally, dialectical theory and Zen philosophy have contributed with other unique perspectives (Linehan & Wilks, 2015).
Behavioral Interventions
Behavioral interventions are based on several theoretical constructs drawn from learning theory. These include: a) contiguity, which refers to the association between stimuli and responses that are connected in time and space; b) classical conditioning, in which a reflex or direct response can become associated with a stimulus through experience; c) operant con-
ditioning, which involves the use of reinforcement or punishment to in-crease or decrease the probability of a certain behavior following an ante-cedent stimulus; and d) social learning, in which a behavior can be learned through observation and imitation of others (Davey, 1998).
A Functional Analysis of Pain and Behavior
CBT practitioners are typically trained to assess cognitive and behav-ioral patterns before suggesting relevant treatment goals and interventions to the patient. There are several assessment approaches depending on the theoretical underpinnings and suggested key mechanisms of treatment. A commonly used approach is referred to as doing a functional analysis (Lin-coln et al., 2017; Rummel et al., 2012). To introduce the theoretical frame-

*The functional analysis, illustrated in Figure 1, primarily aims to iden-tify: 1) relevant situations, antecedents, and triggers of behavioral patterns; 2) cognitive, physiological, and behavioral responses; and 3) reinforcing or punishing consequences (Lincoln et al., 2017; Rummel et al., 2012). Pain, whether chronic or acute, can serve several functions in the analysis. The concepts presented within the illustrated model are highlighted in italics in the upcoming section.*
