Emotion Regulation in Pain
16
In experimental studies, pain is often used as a form of punishing con-
sequence (SP+), and research has consistently demonstrated that pain can decrease the frequency of behavioral responses (R) in both mice and hu-mans (Jean-Richard-Dit-Bressel et al., 2018). While some clinicians be-lieve that pain can be a classically conditioned response (R) to non-noxious stimuli (S), there is little evidence to support this claim (Madden & Mose-ley, 2016). However, pain can be amplified by learning processes, and it has been shown that pain-related responses (e.g., stress, tension, and avoid-
ance) can be conditioned (Madden et al., 2016; Sandström et al., 2020). Therefore, pain and pain-related events are often seen as discriminative stimuli (SD), indicating that certain consequences are available (e.g., in-
creased pain or pain relief), hence triggering a chain of reactions or re-sponses (e.g., hypervigilance, catastrophizing, stress, tension, and avoid-
ance) aimed at obtaining pain relief or avoiding more pain (Vlaeyen & Lin-ton, 2012).
Pain can also be viewed as a motivating operation, with indirect effects on the organism's reactions in several situations, increased probability of
pain-related behavioral responses, as well as altering the value of several
consequences that might be more or less appealing in the presence of pain (Langthorne & McGill, 2009). In addition, pain-related cognitions, and in-formation processing (impulses, expectations, and catastrophizing) could have effects on the interpretation of stimuli, physiological, and behavioral responses, as well as the value and impact of consequences (Dobson & Dozois, 2019; Lincoln et al., 2017; Turk & Gatchel, 2002).
Operant Interventions
Both chronic pain and depression frequently entail avoidance behav-iors, negative thinking, lack of engagement in meaningful activities, and reduced contact with positive experiences (Arnow et al., 2011; Linton & Bergbom, 2011). Operant interventions are based on principles of operant conditioning, and emphasize the influence of context and consequences on these behavioral patterns (Vlaeyen & Crombez, 2020).
Examples of operant interventions for chronic pain is operant behav-
ioral therapy (OBT) and graded activity (GA). OBT aims to produce in-creased function by following targeted overt well-behaviors (i.e., related to increased function and quality of life) with positive reinforcement to in-crease the frequency of these behaviors. Problematic pain behaviors (e.g., expressions of hurting, limping, grimacing, and use of therapeutic devices and medicine in attempts to control pain) are understood as consequences of negative reinforcement (pain-relief) and escape-avoidance conditioning. Hence, interventions also include systematic removal of reinforcers of pain
behavior, as well as classical conditioning methods such as exposure (Turk
Introduction
17
& Gatchel, 2002; Vlaeyen & Crombez, 2020). GA is based on the same prin-ciples as OBT regarding reinforcement of healthy behaviors. In addition, GA aims to gradually increase activity regardless of pain symptoms, incor-porating principles of pacing, i.e., finding a balance between activity and rest to avoid overexertion, and quota management, i.e., setting and track-ing specific goals for graded activity levels (Macedo et al., 2010).
Behavioral Activation (BA) is an operant intervention developed for moderate to severe depression. BA assumes that depression is related to the loss or reduction of positive reinforcement, which weakens behaviors, leading to increased passivity and avoidance patterns. As in OBT and GA, the treatment implies reinforcing functional behaviors and activating the patient to maintain contact with positive reinforcers. Reinforcement in BA is not only defined in terms of what is enjoyable, but also what brings a sense of mastery, satisfaction, and is related to important values (Kanter et al., 2010).
Exposure Therapy
Exposure therapy, originally developed for anxiety disorders, is based on principles of classical conditioning. The assumption is that extinction or reduction of conditioned responses (i.e., fear, stress, and tension) is pos-sible through repeated exposure of the situation (or discriminative stimuli) without the negative consequences that was present during fear-learning (Vinograd & Craske, 2020). These principles are also the foundation of the
fear-avoidance model of pain (Vlaeyen & Linton, 2012). According to this model, pain catastrophizing generates fear that leads to hypervigilance, avoidance behaviors, and subsequent disability and depression. The model advocates that fear of pain can be more disabling than pain itself, and that reduction of pain threat value should decrease disability. Therefore, the model proposes interventions such as exposure, repeatedly engaging in avoided activities to decrease fears and dysfunctional responses (Nicholas et al., 2013; Vlaeyen & Crombez, 2020).
According to emotional processing theory, exposure can modify cogni-tive structures by activating associations and provide new information that disconfirms unrealistic expectations (Kaczkurkin & Foa, 2015). This aligns with findings indicating that it can be effective maximize mismatch with expectations regarding catastrophic outcomes during exposure (McMillan & Lee, 2010; Weisman & Rodebaugh, 2018). On a similar note, research on exposure therapy in chronic pain suggests that, rather than erasing or di-minishing escape-avoidance conditioning, pain patients may learn excep-tions to the rule that certain movements are harmful during exposure (De Peuter et al., 2011).
Emotion Regulation in Pain
18
It is, however, important to emphasize that pain patients do not neces-sarily perceive avoidance responses as unreasonable, they do not generally show anxiety-related brain activation patterns, and many do not report sig-nificant levels of catastrophizing, fear, or disability (Wideman et al., 2013). In other words, avoidance of feared movements only represents one of many behavioral patterns, and pain patients can learn avoidance behaviors without fear or catastrophizing being present.
Cognitive Interventions
Several theoretically based approaches have been developed to under-stand and assess the impact of cognitive patterns and information pro-cessing on behavior. Some approaches assume that humans process infor-mation through cognitive schemas, or core beliefs, which can have altering effects on interpretations of stimuli, physiological, and behavioral re-sponses, as well as the value and impact of consequences (De Houwer et al., 2016). Other CBT-approaches, often referred to as third-generation CBT, focus on changing the awareness and relationship to thoughts rather than the content, and teach patients how to respond differently in situa-tions where thinking becomes dysfunctional. In these treatments metacog-
nitive awareness, or the ability to take a perspective on one’s inner experi-ence, is regarded as a key component (Springer et al., 2011; Hayes & Duck-worth, 2006).
Socratic Dialogue and Behavioral Experiments
CBT therapists aiming to investigate and alter cognitions often use methods such as Socratic dialogue and behavioral experiments. Both ap-proaches entail that the therapist and patient work together to explore be-liefs and assumptions (Dobson & Dozois, 2019). The Socratic dialogue con-sists of verbally exploring important cognitions using questions, summar-ies, and reflections. The aim is to increase awareness of relevant cognitions, reflect upon them, and achieve insights that might help the patient to draw useful conclusions (Clark & Egan, 2015). Behavioral experiments consist of eliciting beliefs regarding outcomes of a specific behavior, designing an experiment to test relevant assumptions, evaluate the outcome, and if needed adjust and repeat the experiment (Bennett-Levy et al., 2004). This approach is often used in exposure therapies to increase the probability of violating expectancies (McMillan & Lee, 2010; Gatzounis et al., 2021; Vlae-yen et al., 2012).
Introduction
19
Metacognitive Awareness
The ability to take perspective on one’s inner experience can be referred to using different terms (e.g., metacognitive awareness, decentering, de-fusion, or distancing), each capturing a slightly different aspect of the pro-cess. The goal of cultivating this type of awareness is to help individuals observe their thoughts from a more objective and non-judgmental stance, allowing for more effective regulation of their behavior (Johannsen et al., 2022). Several techniques to practice this ability have been developed and evaluated within CBT for patients with chronic pain (Chiesa & Serretti, 2011b; Cramer et al., 2012; McCracken, 2013; Veehof et al., 2016) and psy-chiatric disorders (Chiesa & Serretti, 2011a; Johannsen et al., 2022; Nor-mann & Morina, 2018).
Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), developed by Linehan and col-leagues in 1991, uses a similar approach, cultivating metacognitive aware-ness through mindfulness practice (Linehan et al., 1991). In addition, DBT incorporates a dialectical stance to thinking, where every thought or belief (thesis) is assumed to have an equally valid alternative perspective (antith-esis). For example, in DBT, the belief “I need change”, would also be exam-ined from the alternative perspective of “I need acceptance”. By embracing this dialectical stance, individuals are encouraged to consider multiple per-spectives and recognize that two seemingly opposing thoughts or beliefs can both be true at the same time. This can help individuals develop greater flexibility in their thinking (Lynch et al., 2006).
Emotion Regulation Emotion regulation has been suggested as a transdiagnostic factor in
psychopathologies and chronic pain (Linton, 2013; Sloan et al., 2017). It is a complex construct that involves various behaviors and processes, such as recognizing and expressing emotions, and inhibiting dysfunctional re-sponses (Gross, 2002).
What is an Emotion?
How we define and understand emotions can have implications for our understanding of emotion regulation. Most definitions of emotional re-sponses refer to several components including subjective experiences, such as emotional valence (i.e., perceiving an event as positive or negative); ex-pressive behavior (e.g., approach or avoidance); and physiological pro-cesses, such as activity in the autonomic nervous system (i.e., arousal) sug-gested to reflect motor preparation and action tendency (Kreibig, 2010).
Emotion Regulation in Pain
20
Basic emotion models argue that each emotion is caused by a specific mechanism with a particular mental state. From this perspective, distin-guishing between emotion generation (the processes involved in generat-ing an emotional experience) and emotion regulation (the processes in-volved in regulating an initiated emotion generation process) is more straightforward since there is a clear distinction between emotion genera-tors and control systems (Gross et al., 2011; Levenson, 2011).
In appraisal models, emotions are viewed as acts of meaning making with unique function, but no specific mechanisms. Variability in how emo-tions are expressed and experienced are expected, since they are under-stood to arise from the interaction between a situation, appraisal, and pos-sible responses (Barrett et al., 2006; Gross et al., 2011).
In psychological construction models, emotions are not separated from cognition and perception, and seen as a product of these ingredients rather than something specific (Barrett, 2013). From this perspective, it can be difficult to separate emotion generation from regulation, as emotions cannot be regulated but their components can be modified, potentially changing the resulting emotion. Indeed, unitary approaches recognizing that the same processes are involved in emotion generation and regulation have been suggested (Campos et al., 2004).
Last, but not least, social construction models view emotions as prod-ucts of social interaction and culture. From this perspective emotion regu-lation may involve competing social structures or people influencing one another (Boiger & Mesquita, 2012; Gross et al., 2011).
The Process Model of Emotion Regulation
There are several models used to classify and separate emotion regula-tion strategies, some focusing on the outcomes, others on when they have their impact, or if they imply attempts to avoid, control, or accept emotions (Gratz et al., 2015). Even though it is still unclear what system of categori-zation may prove most useful, strategies could differentiate into a limitless amount without any attempt to provide a structure (Gross, 2014).
The process model of emotion regulation (Gross, 1998b, 1998a) cate-gorizes strategies according to when they have their impact in the process of emotional responses. At the base of the process model lies the modal
model of emotion generation, i.e., the situation-attention-appraisal-re-sponse approach from appraisal models of emotion (Gross, 2014). In this model, strategies are categorized as: 1) situation selection, avoidance or confrontation of a situation; 2) situation modification, altering the situa-tion to modify its emotional impact; 3) attentional deployment, selecting what information we attend to; 4) reappraisal, cognitive changes regard-ing our perspective and understanding of the situation; and 5) response
Introduction
21
modulation, altering experiential, physiological or behavioral responses by for example using drugs, relaxation techniques, and expressing or supress-ing emotions. In theory, although these different families of strategies are hypothesized to be sequential milliseconds and seconds before or following an emotional response or potentially emotion-eliciting situation, they could be used in parallel or any order hours or days following the situation (Pena-Sarrionandia et al., 2015).
Complementary Perspectives
In addition to the process model, there are several perspectives often taken into consideration when describing emotion regulation strategies. For instance, it can be of importance to consider if the regulation process involves deliberate and conscious efforts to manage emotions, or if it occurs automatically and unconsciously without awareness or intention. In other words, if the goals are explicit or implicit and the process is controlled or
automatic. In theory, strategies like reappraisal, distraction, and selective attention are often considered more explicit and effortful, while updating the emotional significance of a stimulus through reinforcement and asso-ciative learning is typically described as an automatic and implicit process. However, controlled strategies might become more automatic and effort-less with practice, and implicit goals could become explicit in certain con-texts (Braunstein et al., 2017).
It is also important to assess if strategies can be considered functional or dysfunctional, often referred to as adaptive or maladaptive. In other words, how well the consequences of using the strategy in a specific context correspond to personal values and goals. We can fail to functionally regu-late emotions in several ways. In some situations, we might not identify the need to regulate due to attentional deployment and lack of interoceptive awareness. In other situations, we may have difficulties identifying what strategy to use, or how to implement them related to lack of skill, overuse of specific strategies, or low self-efficacy. Fortunately, it seems that many of these factors can be modified (Gross, 2014, 2015; Sloan et al., 2017).
Another approach is to differentiate between disengagement strate-
gies (such as distraction and situation modification, avoiding experiences) and engagement strategies (such as mindful awareness and cognitive re-appraisal, engaging in the experience). It has been found that we often pre-fer disengagement strategies when unpleasant experiences are more in-tense (Van Bockstaele et al., 2020). Indeed, it has been suggested that when faced with a challenging situation, temporarily using distraction to cope with emotions may be functional in the short term. However, in the long run, it may be more beneficial to follow up with an engagement strategy, such as reappraisal, to more effectively manage the emotions associated with the situation (Gross & John, 2003).
Emotion Regulation in Pain
22
An Acceptance-Based Definition of Emotion Regulation
Acceptance is a broad term that has been written about for centuries from the Buddhist Sutras, the New Testament, and philosophers such as Aurelius and Kierkegaard, to psychologists such as Ellis, Freud, Skinner, Rogers, and Hayes (Williams & Lynn, 2010). Some researchers have argued that acceptance is best defined as attempts not to regulate emotions (Black-ledge & Hayes, 2001). However, this depends on the definition of emotion regulation. If it is defined as efforts to control the intensity and duration of emotional experiences, the perspectives may indeed be incoherent. In con-trast, there are approaches emphasising that adaptive emotion regulation involves the ability to engage in goal-directed behaviors when experiencing emotions rather than experiential avoidance. This functional approach of-ten involves developing acceptance (Gratz & Tull, 2010).
The definition of emotion regulation by Gratz and Roemer (2004) is designed to be clinically useful for development and modification of treat-ments. It highlights the importance of adaptive responses to emotional dis-tress (including being aware, understanding, and accepting emotions); the need for self-control in managing impulsive behaviors; and the flexible use of contextually appropriate strategies to modulate emotional responses based on personal goals and situational demands (Gratz et al., 2015).
Emotion Regulation and Pain Emotions and pain interact, with pain inducing emotions and emotions
affecting pain perception. Pain is strongly related to avoidance or defensive actions, and elicits related emotional responses. In addition, negative emo-tions generally intensify pain perception, while positive emotions reduce it. This effect occurs regardless of the emotion's relation to pain, and strength-ens with increased emotional intensity (Rhudy, 2016).
Several studies support the idea that emotion regulation can entail ef-fects on pain intensity as well as resilience, i.e., the ability to engage in be-haviors despite pain (Aaron et al., 2020, 2022; Gentili et al., 2019; Lumley et al., 2011; Vowles et al., 2007). Furthermore, emotion regulation has been found to predict pain modulation (Lapate et al., 2012), and maladaptive response-focused emotion regulation strategies have been found to be as-sociated with chronic pain and pain-related disability (Koechlin et al., 2018).
Wiech et al. (2008) suggested that pain itself can be perceived as a reg-ulatable emotion, since attention, expectation, and reappraisal are essen-tial factors of the pain experience. The authors also demonstrated how these processes can play a role in inducing placebo-based pain relief though
Introduction
23
different neural pathways. While acknowledging the possibility of addi-tional pain modulation mechanisms, they emphasize that attentional de-ployment and cognitive reappraisal processes are likely to be involved in some capacity. In the following section, I provide a brief overview of find-ings derived from laboratory studies that have explored effects of emotion regulation strategies on acute and experimentally induced pain.
Attentional Deployment and Pain
Distraction and Shifting Focus
Pain is an experience that attracts attention (Eccleston & Crombez, 1999). It has the capacity to draw focus away from daily activities (Johnson, 2005), and entail performance issues in attention demanding tasks (Robi-son et al., 2021). The ability to shift focus from pain and private experiences to other stimuli, often entitled distraction, has been shown to be an effec-tive regulation strategy in some contexts. Birnie et al. (2017) provide a brief introduction to different theoretical approaches on this topic. In summary, distraction may reduce pain perception by using up limited attentional ca-pacity. In addition, it might be more effective when competing for the same perceptual and spatial resources.
Distraction has been associated with lower pain intensity and higher completion rates than focused attention in pain tolerance tests (Nouwen et al., 2006; Rischer et al., 2020; Van Damme et al., 2008), regardless of ex-ecutive abilities to shift and regulate attention (Verhoeven et al., 2011). Moreover, directing focus away from pain locations can have effects on pain tolerance (Van Ryckeghem et al., 2011), and pain unpleasantness (Cioffi & Holloway, 1993). However, there are also findings indicating that distraction during activities can be associated with increased post-activity pain (Goubert et al., 2004). In addition, studies have found that while dis-traction may be effective in reducing acute and experimentally induced pain, it does not show positive long-term effects in chronic pain conditions (Van Ryckeghem et al., 2018).
It has been argued that distraction should be differentiated from sup-pression (Masedo & Esteve, 2007), and that distraction may be adaptive when combined with acceptance, but maladaptive when applied with avoidance (Wolgast & Lundh, 2017). Several authors also emphasize that distraction from pain can prove to be difficult, depending on variables such as pain intensity (Buhle & Wager, 2010). Another important aspect to con-sider is the heterogeneity of distractors used in different studies. It is prob-able that shifting focus towards meaningful non-pain goals may be more effective than simply trying to shift focus away from unpleasant sensations (Schrooten et al., 2012).
Emotion Regulation in Pain
24
Attentional Bias and Threat Interpretations
It has been suggested that a rigid and excessive focus on bodily sensa-tions may play a central role in the development and maintenance of chronic pain (Crombez et al., 2013). Indeed, research has shown that indi-viduals with chronic pain can exhibit attentional bias towards pain-related information, and this may predict pain interference (Todd et al., 2023). However, other factors seem to moderate these effects. For instance, Broadbent et al. (2022) argued that negative effects of attentional bias could be moderated by threat-related interpretations (i.e., perceiving the information in a manner that emphasize potential harm, danger, or other negative consequences). Since motivation and attention are closely con-nected, pain-related goals such as trying to control pain could lead to in-creased processing of pain-related information (Van Damme et al., 2010). Consequently, avoidance-related emotional responses like anxiety, worry, and judgmental thinking may entail increased focus towards pain. There-fore, focusing on acceptance and reappraisal of pain-related beliefs might be more effective than modulating attentional bias in chronic pain treat-ments (Broadbent et al., 2022).
Reappraisal and Pain
Individuals with chronic pain may develop negative beliefs and expec-tations about their pain, leading to cognitive biases and maladaptive coping strategies. This, in turn, can increase their pain perception, leading to a vi-cious cycle of pain and distress (Eccleston & Crombez, 1999). The misdi-rected problem-solving model suggests that pain catastrophizing comes from a human tendency to ruminate on negative outcomes and escape strategies. This creates a cycle of anxiety and ineffective problem-solving attempts that could be reinforced by approaches focusing on pain relief. Hence, it has been suggested that shifting focus to functional goals might entail better treatment outcomes (Linton & Shaw, 2011).
While evidence suggests that cognitive processes and threat-related re-sponses can have an impact on pain perception, this effect is typically lim-ited and varies greatly among individuals (Wiech et al., 2008). On a similar note, while studies have shown that reappraisal strategies can modulate the perception of experimental pain (Adamczyk et al., 2020; Hampton et al., 2015; Lapate et al., 2012; Woo et al., 2015), the effects of these strategies may not always be present in longer lasting pain tests (Denson et al., 2014; Hovasapian & Levine, 2016). Nevertheless, self-efficacy (i.e., an individu-al's belief in their ability to successfully perform specific tasks or achieve goals) has been associated with pain intensity (Wiech et al., 2008). Fur-thermore, it has been suggested that changing how we think about pain might entail remembering it as less intense, which could prevent the devel-opment of avoidance behaviors (Hovasapian & Levine, 2016).
Introduction
25
Acceptance and Pain
Acceptance has been found to be more predictive of outcomes such as pain-related anxiety, depression, disability, and work status, than pain in-tensity alone in chronic pain conditions (Hayes & Duckworth, 2006; McCracken, 1998; McCracken & Zhao-O’Brien, 2010). In addition, findings from several studies suggest that acceptance training may be more efficient to increase tolerance of experimentally induced pain than reappraisal strat-egies (Kohl et al., 2013) and distraction (Gutiérrez et al., 2004; Jackson et al., 2012; McMullen et al., 2008), at least among participants who fre-quently employ acceptance as their coping style (Moore et al., 2015).
While some studies have demonstrated the impact of acceptance on pain intensity compared to suppression and control-based coping (Braams et al., 2012; Keogh et al., 2005; Masedo & Esteve, 2007; Paez-Blarrina et al., 2008), it appears that these exercises may not be as effective in reduc-ing pain intensity as distraction techniques (Kohl et al., 2013). Another no-table finding is that suppression by itself, which is considered an opposite to acceptance, has been associated with higher distress and pain intensity in experimental settings (Brockman et al., 2017; Masedo & Esteve, 2007; Olatunji et al., 2017). However, Braams et al. (2012), found that while ac-ceptance entailed greater reductions in anticipatory anxiety towards elec-trical shocks, both suppression and anxiety were more effective than spon-taneous coping on pain intensity and cardiac defence responses.
The acceptance training used in experimental studies often include in-structions and exercises related to non-judgmental metacognitive aware-ness, willingness to experience discomfort, and refraining from experien-tial avoidance. Based on descriptions of the exercises, it appears that met-acognitive awareness (in this context referred to as cognitive defusion) might be the most prominent component (Hayes et al., 1999; Kohl et al., 2012; Wojnarowska et al., 2020). However, since these processes are as-sumed to be interconnected and overlapping, they are typically studied in combination rather than in isolation (Hayes et al., 2012; Shapiro et al., 2006). In accordance with this assumption, McMullen et al. (2008) found that more extensive acceptance training, including both experiential exer-cises and metaphors, was needed to find a positive effect on task tolerance. It has also been suggested that acceptance strategies may be more effective on pain tolerance together with other aspects of treatments, such as contact with important values and goals (Branstetter-Rost et al., 2009; Paez-Blar-rina et al., 2008).
Regarding acceptance and attentional deployment, Wang et al. (2019) found that acceptance training was effective on pain tolerance with and without directing attention towards pain sensations. In addition, ac-ceptance training alone was more effective than merely the latter, which had no impact on tolerance without acceptance.
Emotion Regulation in Pain
26
Mindfulness and Pain
Several studies have evaluated the effects of mindfulness exercises, in-tegrating both attention training and acceptance strategies. In a recent re-view on the effect of mindfulness-based interventions on acute pain, Shires et al. (2020) concluded that there is moderate evidence that mindfulness exercises have effects on pain tolerance, and weak evidence of effects on pain threshold on experimentally induced pain. However, no significant ef-fects were found on pain intensity or pain-related distress in clinical or ex-perimental settings.
McClintock et al. (2019) differentiated exercises by duration and method of delivery and concluded that brief mindfulness exercises led by a practitioner have shown more consistent effects than audio-recorded exer-cises. Practitioner led exercises have shown positive effects on pain toler-ance, pain threshold, and reduced pain anxiety during cold-pressor tests (Burnett et al., 2017); pain intensity ratings during electrical stimulation of the arm (Zeidan et al., 2010); and pain threshold, pain intensity, and pain unpleasantness during heat stimulation (Reiner et al., 2016; Zeidan et al., 2011, 2015, 2016). Although audio recorded exercises have shown positive effects of on pain tolerance compared to spontaneous coping during cold pressor tests (Evans et al., 2014; Forsyth & Hayes, 2014; Liu et al., 2013), effects are inconclusive on pain threshold and distress compared to spon-taneous coping and distraction (Forsyth & Hayes, 2014; Liu et al., 2013; Shires et al., 2019), and pain tolerance compared to guided imagery (King-ston et al., 2007; Petter et al., 2013). In addition, no effects have been found for audio recorded exercises compared to hypnosis (Swain & Trevena, 2014), relaxation (Sharpe et al., 2013), reading (Petter et al., 2014), or lis-tening to fairy tales (Prins et al., 2014).
Regarding acute effects of brief mindfulness exercises among patients experiencing pain, several studies have found positive effects on pain-re-lated distress compared to psychoeducation, relaxation, and other control conditions (Coelho et al., 2018; Duncan et al., 2017; Feuille & Pargament, 2015; Garland, Baker, et al., 2017; Ratcliff et al., 2019; Ussher et al., 2014). Although some studies have found positive effects on pain intensity (Gar-land, Baker, et al., 2017; Soo et al., 2016), others have failed to confirm these findings (Coelho et al., 2018; Ratcliff et al., 2019; Warth et al., 2015).
Avoidance and Pain-Related Fear Learning
Dysfunctional emotion regulation and avoidance could influence both associative and operant learning among patients with chronic pain (Cor-dier & Diers, 2018). Studies on pain-related fear learning (van Vliet et al., 2018; Zaman et al., 2015) provide several findings suggesting that disen-
gagement strategies and avoiding unpleasant stimuli can be problematic.
Introduction
27
For instance, avoidance is often related to inadequate generalization of re-sponses, difficulties to differentiate between stimulus and contexts, and er-roneously explaining absence of danger to avoidance behaviors. Further-more, the possibility to avoid pain seem to trigger more avoidance re-sponses and behaviors, vigilance, and increased threat level. This could de-velop into a negative spiral of emotion dysregulation, both maintaining and exacerbating pain and emotional distress. From this perspective, func-tional emotion regulation strategies might lower the threat level of pain-related stimuli and counteract problematic learning processes. In addition, engagement or approach strategies could increase possibilities to learn to differentiate between stimulus and contexts, thereby less inadequate gen-eralization of responses. For example, a recent study showed that mindful awareness (an engagement strategy) implied reduced spontaneous recov-ery of threat responses the day after fear learning (Bjorkstrand et al., 2019).
Emotion Regulation in Therapy Although the term emotion regulation may not be explicitly used, vir-
tually all forms of CBT incorporate interventions that involve emotion reg-ulation strategies, such as relaxation training, acceptance, or cognitive re-appraisal. In addition, most therapies advice against frequent use of mala-daptive disengagement strategies and experiential avoidance (O’Donohue
& Fisher, 2012). In a recent systematic review, Sloan et al. (2017) found that maladaptive emotion regulation decreased significantly in most studies measuring this aspect, regardless of disorder or the specific CBT treatment being used.
Dialectical Behavior Therapy (Linehan, 1993), Emotion Regulation Therapy (Mennin, 2006), Affect Regulation Training (Berking & Lukas, 2015), Emotion Regulation Group Therapy (Gratz & Gunderson, 2006), and the hybrid transdiagnostic exposure treatment (Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014), are examples of CBT-treatments explicitly targeting emotion regu-lation skills with an underlying hypothesis that this might improve other important aspects such as health, function, and quality of life. Several of these treatments are based on principles from mindfulness and ac-ceptance-based interventions (Gratz & Gunderson, 2006; Linehan, 1993; Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014).
Mindfulness and Acceptance-Based CBT
Mindfulness and acceptance-based interventions share a strong con-nection, as both prioritize non-judgmental present moment awareness, perspective taking, and valued action. Research on acceptance frequently includes mindfulness as a component, and acceptance is regarded as a fun-damental aspect of mindfulness. Therefore, it is useful to explore both
Emotion Regulation in Pain
28
mindfulness and acceptance research when studying either approach (Al-dao et al., 2010; Gratz & Tull, 2010; Kohl et al., 2012).
Various forms of CBT incorporate acceptance and mindfulness tech-niques as key components for treating affective disorders and chronic pain (Johannsen et al., 2022; Veehof et al., 2016). These approaches are often grounded in behavioral principles and learning theories, such as Ac-ceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), Mindfulness-based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) and Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), utilizing expo-sure practices, goal setting, values clarification, and reinforcement princi-ples (Hayes et al., 2006; Lynch et al., 2006; Segal et al., 2018). Additionally, these interventions involve developing metacognitive awareness (Lynch et al., 2006; Teasdale et al., 2002), or cognitive defusion (Hayes et al., 2012).
Dialectical Behavior Therapy
Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) was developed for highly suicidal patients with emotion regulation difficulties. It integrates mindfulness skills translated from Zen practices with behavioral principles and learning theory. The therapy has a clear emphasis on emotion regulation training, using strategies such as acceptance, metacognitive awareness, and re-sponse modulation to increase functioning (Linehan & Wilks, 2015). In ac-cordance with acceptance-based definitions of emotion regulation, DBT educates patients that emotions are natural, temporary, and evolved re-sponses to both internal and external stimuli. The emotion regulation training in DBT aims to teach patients how to identify and describe their emotions, reduce vulnerability to negative emotions, and effectively regu-late emotional responses.
In a conceptual review by Lynch et al., (2006) the authors propose that mindfulness, opposite action, behavioral targeting, chain analysis, and di-alectics all work to create change by a) eliminating ineffective emotional responses using exposure and response prevention; b) learning new effec-tive responses to emotional stimuli; c) improving attentional control, stim-ulus discrimination, or memory; and d) balancing and sustaining effective strategies through the dialectic approach. The authors emphasize that these mechanisms probably work together in a dynamic way and have a synergistic effect in improving treatment outcomes.
DBT skills training involves didactic instruction and utilizes various methods such as modelling, feedback, coaching, homework assignments, and storytelling. The therapy consists of four skill modules, including mindfulness, interpersonal effectiveness, emotional regulation, and dis-tress tolerance. These modules are divided into change skills (e.g., emo-tional regulation and interpersonal effectiveness) and acceptance skills (e.g., mindfulness, self-compassion, and distress tolerance).
Introduction
29
DBT places a significant emphasis on mindfulness, which is regarded as the ‘core skill’. The mindfulness skill module provides rationale and ed-ucation on the significance of mindfulness training and includes work-sheets for tracking and assessing training sessions. Moreover, other skill modules in DBT also integrate at least one mindfulness skill (Linehan & Wilks, 2015).
Mechanisms of Mindfulness Several theoretical frameworks have been proposed to identify key
components of mindfulness-based interventions (Baer, 2003; Carmody, n.d.; Chambers et al., 2009; Day et al., 2014; Garland et al., 2015; Goldberg, 2022; Harrison et al., 2017; Hill & Updegraff, 2012; Holzel et al., 2011; Shapiro et al., 2006; Zeidan & Vago, 2016). Regardless of approach, most frameworks suggest that mindfulness-based interventions involve cultivat-ing acceptance, developing skills to accept and observe thoughts, feelings, and sensations without judgment or reactivity; training attentional con-
trol, improving flexibility in controlling, maintaining, and shifting atten-tion; and expanding awareness to previously unattended internal and ex-ternal stimuli.
Different Mindfulness-Based Practices
Chiesa & Malinowski (2011), provide a comparative analysis of the phil-osophical underpinnings, objectives, techniques, and proposed mecha-nisms of various mindfulness-based approaches. Their analysis reveals sig-nificant differences in the ways mindfulness is conceptualized and prac-ticed. While MBCT emphasizes formal meditation practice, other ap-proaches such as ACT and DBT do not necessarily include it. Instead, these approaches use metaphors and brief mindfulness-based exercises to teach specific skills such as observing, describing, participating, being non-judg-mental, mindful, and effective in DBT (Linehan & Wilks, 2015); or being present, taking perspective, and choosing valued action in ACT (Hayes et al., 2012).
When comparing mindfulness interventions, it is also important to consider the type of attention training being utilized. The different ap-proaches can be broadly classified into two main styles: focused attention, which involves sustained focus for longer periods on a specific object (for example mindful breathing or body scan); and open monitoring, which en-tails non-reactive observation of moment-to-moment experience (Manna et al., 2010). Although mindfulness-based treatments usually incorporate both forms of attention training, the extent to which they emphasize each style may vary. In a meta-analysis on mindfulness as attention training,
Emotion Regulation in Pain
30
Verhaeghen (2020) concluded that attention performance may be im-proved by mindfulness training, with more consistent effects on sustained attention and inhibition than updating and shifting. Despite the lack of sig-nificant differences between different types of meditative practices, the studies that incorporated focused-attention techniques were the only ones with significant effects on these outcomes. Therefore, the author suggested that attention training focusing on one or more specific locations or stimuli might be essential to enhance attentional control.
Mindfulness and Emotion Regulation Several authors have attempted to incorporate mindfulness and ac-
ceptance in the process model of emotion regulation as attentional deploy-ment (Pena-Sarrionandia et al., 2015; Slutsky et al., 2017), cognitive change (Naragon-Gainey et al., 2017; Pena-Sarrionandia et al., 2015; Webb et al., 2012), and response modulation (Farb et al., 2014; Block-Lerner et al. 2009). In addition, Buddhists, Stoics, and psychologists have characterized acceptance as the willingness to act despite discomfort (Williams & Lynn, 2010), and acceptance measures often include statements like, “I do the things I want to do even if it makes me feel nervous or anxious” (Wolgast, 2014). Thus, it can be argued that mindfulness and acceptance-based ap-proaches also involve confrontational situation selection (Gross, 2014). In other words, mindfulness appears to encompass nearly the entire range of strategies outlined by the process model.
Mindfulness and Attentional Deployment
Mindfulness exercises often employ an interoceptive focus to foster ac-ceptance for internal experiences (i.e., bodily sensations, thoughts, and emotions), or to use internal sensations (e.g., sensations of breathing) as focal points for attention training (Baer, 2003; Cayoun et al., 2017; De Jong et al., 2016; Dreeben et al., 2013; Kerr et al., 2013; Shapiro et al., 2006). Indeed, several authors suggest that acceptance involve directing focus to-wards something, and engaging fully with events, rather than withdrawing or being distracted (Farb et al., 2014; Slutsky et al., 2017; Block-Lerner et al., 2009).
However, mindfulness rationales also emphasize the importance of non-attachment and letting go while observing internal and external events. Hence, instructions are neither to eliminate nor cling to experiences (Block-Lerner et al., 2009; Kabat-Zinn, 1982; J. C. Williams & Lynn, 2010). Likewise, acceptance measures include questions such as “I let my thoughts
and feelings come and go…” (Wolgast, 2014), and acceptance rationales in experimental research and interventions encourage “open monitoring”
(Pena-Sarrionandia et al., 2015). Consequently, while mindfulness does
Introduction
31
not necessarily imply directing focus towards specific stimuli, it involves openness to experiences, and can entail increased interoceptive and exter-nal awareness.
Interoceptive Awareness
Interoceptive awareness has been suggested as a critical factor in the experience and regulation of emotional responses (Garland et al., 2015; Gibson, 2019; Price & Hooven, 2018; Price & Weng, 2021). It involves the perception and interpretation of sensory information from within the body, emotional appraisal, and inferences about these sensations. This can be di-vided into different domains, such as interoceptive accuracy (i.e., the ability to detect internal states) and interoceptive metacognitive awareness (i.e., the cognitive assessment of accuracy). Both aspects have been suggested as key components of mindfulness interventions (Casals-Gutiérrez & Abbey, 2020; Craig, 2004; Gibson, 2019; Price & Weng, 2021).
Since chronic pain can be associated with over-identification and emo-tional reactivity to pain, it has been suggested that training disengaged in-teroceptive awareness may be important for pain patients (Cayoun et al., 2017; De Jong et al., 2016). In addition, some findings suggest that individ-uals with chronic pain may experience deficiencies in interoceptive abili-ties, particularly in accurately detecting physiological states. This could po-tentially hinder their capacity to regulate emotions effectively (Di Lernia et al., 2016). However, in a conceptual review, Gibson (2019) suggest that in-teroceptive accuracy does not have a direct impact on well-being since it is also influenced by how individuals subjectively interpret their bodily sen-sations. Indeed, directing attention internally may not always be beneficial in chronic pain when it can be related to hypervigilance and threat inter-pretations (Crombez et al., 2013). In addition, when combined with nega-tive thoughts, excessive focus towards the self has also been linked to in-creased emotional distress in other disorders (Michael & Burns, 2004; Mor & Winquist, 2002; Villemure & Bushnell, 2002).
Exteroceptive Awareness
There are mindfulness exercises aiming to increase exteroceptive
awareness, such as mindful listening directing focus externally towards sounds (Baer, 2003). These interventions have been shown to be effective on negative and ruminative thinking, emotional distress, and attentional biases, among healthy samples and individuals with psychiatric disorders (Fergus et al., 2014; Callinan et al., 2015; Taraban et al., 2016; Knowles et al., 2016; Loo et al., 2020). Less is known about the effects of mindfulness exercises with external focus in chronic pain. However, studies training at-
Emotion Regulation in Pain
32
tentional control from other theoretical perspectives have shown that di-recting focus towards external stimuli during training can have positive acute effects on pain intensity, pain unpleasantness, and pain threshold in experimentally induced pain (Bascour-Sandoval et al., 2019; Sharpe et al., 2010; Sloan & Hollins, 2017).
Mindfulness and Reappraisal
Mindfulness practice involves encouraging and training acceptance and metacognitive awareness (Shapiro et al., 2006; J. C. Williams & Lynn, 2010). In contrast to cognitive reappraisal of the emotional experience or situation, acceptance has been conceptualized as reappraising judgemental thinking regarding our emotional responses (Naragon-Gainey et al., 2017; Wolgast et al., 2011). In addition, metacognitive awareness has been con-ceptualized as a distinct form of reappraisal, separate from other strategies that involve reinterpretation of emotional stimuli (Webb et al., 2012; Pena-Sarrionandia et al., 2015). Some authors have suggested that acceptance may be less difficult to employ than other reappraisal strategies (Troy et al., 2019; Wenzel, 2023). Moreover, it has been proposed that mindfulness could facilitate positive reappraisal of stressors, by increasing metacogni-tive awareness and gaining access to previously unattended sensory infor-mation (Garland, 2015). Indeed, it has been found that levels of mindful-ness achieved during meditation can be associated with increased use of reappraisal strategies (Garland et al., 2013, Roberts et al., 2021).
In addition to metacognitive awareness and acceptance, mindfulness-based approaches including MBCT and DBT, also emphasize practicing self-compassion (Wilson et al., 2019). While this strategy has been de-scribed as less focused on modifying thoughts than other forms of cognitive reappraisal (Preuss et al., 2021), the definition involves changing cogni-tions towards self-kindness rather than self-criticism (Neff, 2003). In ad-dition, some findings indicate that self-compassion can be related to the use and effectiveness of other reappraisal strategies in depression and so-cial anxiety (Diedrich et al., 2016; Bates et al., 2021).
Mindfulness and Response Modulation
Mindfulness includes several concepts related to modulating behav-ioral responses including non-doing, observing impulses to act without act-ing; non-attachment, not clinging to experiences; and non-avoidance, not following impulses to avoid experiences (Williams & Lynn, 2010). Thus, mindfulness involves abstaining from both experiential and behavioral re-sponse modulation (Gross, 2014), neither engaging in nor suppressing emotional experiences. Likewise, acceptance training in experimental re-search often includes instructions to refrain from impulses to control, mod-ify, or intervene, and not allow thoughts and feelings to dictate behavior
Introduction
33
(Wojnarowska et al., 2020). Indeed, acceptance has been defined as a re-sponse-focused regulation strategy (Block-Lerner et al., 2009).
Regarding physiological response modulation, some responses such as hyperventilating and tensing muscles could be closely related to struggling and avoidance (Van Vliet et al., 2018). Hence, since mindfulness and ac-ceptance imply abstaining from these impulses, it is not surprising these approaches may entail lowered arousal (Hofmann et al., 2009). However, this effect might not be immediate (Björkstrand et al., 2019), and it is im-portant to emphasize that there is a difference between doing something to achieve relaxation and simply observing sensations without striving for a particular state. This distinguishes mindfulness-based strategies from re-laxation training and positive reappraisal (Wolgast et al., 2011).
Efficacy of CBT in Pain and Psychiatric Disorders As stated earlier, CBT has substantial empirical support for its effec-
tiveness in psychiatric disorders, with large effects for specific phobias, ob-sessive-compulsive disorder, hypochondriasis, body dysmorphic disorder, and general stress; moderate to large effects for social anxiety; and moder-ate effects for panic disorder, anger problems, eating disorders and depres-sion (Hofmann et al., 2012). A recent review of the efficacy of psychological interventions in chronic pain by Williams et al. (2020), concluded that there is moderate quality evidence for small effects of CBT post-treatment compared to treatment as usual on pain intensity, disability, and distress; and very small effects compared active control conditions. Effects were maintained at follow-up compared to treatment as usual, but not compared to active control.
Behavioral Interventions
Behavioral Activation (BA) has shown positive effects for individuals affected by depression, with positive long-term effects compared to treat-ment as usual and medication (Uphoff et al., 2020). In chronic pain, the evidence for operant interventions is more limited, with recent meta-anal-yses failing to find positive effects of operant behavioral therapy (OBT) and graded activity (GA) on pain intensity, functional status, or distress (Ho et al., 2022; Williams et al., 2020). While Ho et al. (2020) found that these interventions in combination with physiotherapy had positive effects on pain intensity maintained at midterm follow-up, the effect was not per-ceptible for behavioral interventions without physiotherapy. Two previous meta-analyses have found limited evidence of positive long-term effects of GA in chronic low-back pain on pain and disability compared to passive control conditions, but not compared to physical exercise (López-De-Uralde-Villanueva et al., 2016; Macedo et al., 2010).
Emotion Regulation in Pain
34
Regarding exposure therapy, research has consistently shown positive effects on fear and avoidance in anxiety disorders such as obsessive-com-pulsive disorder and specific phobias (Kaczkurkin & Foa, 2015). In addi-tion, results from several studies indicate that exposure therapy might be an effective approach to decrease catastrophizing and avoidance in chronic pain (Flink et al., 2012; Glombiewski et al., 2018; Leeuw et al., 2008; Lin-ton et al., 2008; Nicholas et al., 2013; Schemer et al., 2018; Vlaeyen et al., 2001; Woods & Asmundson, 2008). One meta-analysis concludes that there is moderate quality evidence that exposure therapy for chronic low back pain have more prominent short-term effects on catastrophizing than GA (López-De-Uralde-Villanueva et al., 2016). However, regarding pa-tients with comorbid pain and emotional distress, Flink et al. (2012) found that high levels of catastrophizing predicted lack of improvements from ex-posure, and anxiety was a predictor of poor outcomes in general.
Cognitive Interventions
Several studies have shown that cognitive therapy, focusing on altering dysfunctional beliefs, can be equally effective as exposure therapy for sev-eral anxiety disorders (Kaczkurkin & Foa, 2015). However, the evidence for cognitive therapy without behavioral interventions in chronic pain condi-tions is limited, with one meta-analysis suggesting that there is no evident effect on pain reduction or functional status for patients with chronic low-back pain (Henschke et al., 2010). Nevertheless, it is important to empha-size that most studies supporting the efficacy of CBT for chronic pain em-ploy treatment protocols that incorporate exercises aimed at addressing misdirected or ineffective problem-solving, negative thinking, catastro-phizing, and dysfunctional rule-governed behaviors (Lamb et al., 2010; Linton & Shaw, 2011; van Koulil et al., 2010; Wetherell et al., 2011). In ad-dition, exposure therapy for both specific phobia and chronic pain integrate behavioral experiments and cognitive interventions, aiming to explore and alter beliefs and increase the probability of violating expectancies during exposure (Gatzounis et al., 2021; McMillan & Lee, 2010; Vlaeyen et al., 2012). The hypothesis that changing the impact of dysfunctional beliefs can be an important treatment mechanism is also supported by the findings by Murillo et al. (2022), suggesting that decreased pain-related fear, catastro-phizing, and increased self-efficacy mediate effects of CBT on pain-related disability.
Mindfulness-Based Interventions
Reviews and meta-analyses addressing the efficacy of mindfulness-based interventions in psychiatric conditions, have found moderate to large effects for depression and anxiety disorders (Hofmann & Gómez, 2017; Zhang et al., 2021); and moderate effects for general stress (Zhang et al.,
Introduction
35
2021). In addition, Johannsen et al. (2022) concluded that mindful atten-tion, metacognitive awareness, and acceptance mediated effects of these treatments on primary outcomes.
In chronic pain, meta-analyses have found moderate to large effects of mindfulness-based interventions on functional status (Veehof et al., 2016); and moderate effects on catastrophizing, acceptance, and symptoms of de-pression (Schütze et al., 2018; Ball et al., 2017; Veehof et al., 2016). How-ever, findings are slightly incoherent across reviews, likely due to incon-sistent definitions of mindfulness (Cardle et al., 2023). In addition, meta-analyses on ACT for chronic pain has demonstrated low-quality evidence for positive long-term effects on catastrophizing, acceptance, anxiety, and functional status (Hughes et al., 2017; Schütze et al., 2018; Trindade et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2020). Furthermore, Murillo et al. (2022) concluded that increased acceptance and psychological flexibility (i.e., the ability to stay in contact with the present moment and pursue meaningful goals) seem to mediate the effects of ACT for chronic pain on functional status.
Integrating Knowledge and Approaches Since there are several aspects to consider regarding the heterogeneity
of patients and different treatment perspectives, integrating knowledge and approaches can be a challenging endeavour. Nevertheless, several con-clusions can be drawn from theoretical assumptions and findings described in previous sections.
Interventions Targeting Pain and Emotional Distress
The previous brief review of the evidence makes it clear that while CBT seems to be an effective intervention for both pain and psychiatric disor-ders, effects are generally larger and more consistent for the latter (Hof-mann et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2020).
In theory, exposure in vivo and behavioral experiments could be a use-ful approach when certain contexts elicit fear- and avoidance responses due to learned associations (Vinograd & Craske, 2020; Vlaeyen & Crombez, 2020). Indeed, CBT interventions using these approaches have shown moderate to large effects in several anxiety disorders (Hofmann, 2012; Ka-czkurkin & Foa, 2015). In addition, findings indicate that exposure therapy might be an effective approach to decrease catastrophizing in chronic low-back pain (López-De-Uralde-Villanueva et al., 2016). Likewise, operant in-terventions could theoretically be a useful approach when pain primarily function as negative reinforcement and punishment, entailing depressive symptoms and loss of meaningful positive reinforcement due to pain avoid-ance (Kanter et al., 2008; Linton & Bergbom, 2011). Indeed, interventions
Emotion Regulation in Pain
36
developed to modify these behavioral patterns have shown positive effects in depression (Uphoff et al., 2020). However, there is little support for purely operant interventions in chronic pain (Ho et al., 2022; Williams et al., 2020), and CBT treatment packages for chronic pain combining oper-ant principles with cognitive interventions have shown none to small long-term effects on symptoms of depression (Bernardy et al., 2019; Henschke et al., 2010; Hughes et al., 2017; Williams et al., 2020).
In summary, while treatments based on CBT principles have been proven effective for both chronic pain and psychiatric disorders, the effects of CBT in chronic pain are relatively small. This could be related to ceiling effects due to inclusion of patients with less cognitive and behavioral prob-lems. However, previous findings indicate that CBT might be even less ef-fective among chronic pain patients with higher levels of emotional distress (Flink et al., 2012, 2014). Hence, another plausible explanation is that fo-cusing on pain management may result in insufficient attention and time devoted to emotional problems (Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014).
Enhancing CBT using Emotion Regulation
While it might be premature to draw conclusions on causal relations, research from several fields describe associations between emotional dis-tress and chronic pain (Lumley et al., 2011; Velly & Mohit, 2018). There-fore, it has been suggested that targeting transdiagnostic processes such as emotion regulation could improve outcomes for patients with these comor-bidities (Linton, 2010; Linton & Bergbom, 2011). Indeed, treatments com-bining mindfulness-based strategies with basic CBT-principles have shown positive effects in both psychiatric disorders (Hofmann & Gómez, 2017; Norton et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2021) and chronic pain (Cardle et al., 2023; Hughes et al., 2017; Veehof et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2021). Several studies also suggest that skills training from DBT, used as a stand-alone treatment, may enhance mindfulness and emotion regulation skills in var-ious populations and settings (Valentine et al. 2020). In addition, feasibil-ity studies indicate that incorporating skills training from DBT in chronic pain management may lead to positive impacts on various outcomes in-cluding pain intensity, physical function, emotion dysregulation, depres-sion, catastrophizing, acceptance, negative affect, and opioid use (Barrett et al., 2021; Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014; Norman-Nott et al., 2022).
Regarding the effects of specific emotion regulation strategies, experi-mental studies have shown positive acute effects on pain tolerance of ac-ceptance exercises training non-judgmental metacognitive awareness and refraining from experiential avoidance (Hayes et al., 1999; Kohl et al., 2012; Wojnarowska et al., 2020). In addition, mindfulness exercises, integrating these skills with attention training, have shown positive effects on pain tol-erance and pain threshold (Shires et al., 2020). Some studies also indicate
Introduction
37
that reinterpretative positive reappraisal may have positive effects on the perception of pain (Adamczyk et al., 2020; Hampton et al., 2015; Lapate et al., 2012; Woo et al., 2015). However, these effects may not always be pre-sent in longer lasting pain tests (Denson et al., 2014; Hovasapian & Levine, 2016).
I find it more challenging to briefly review findings on the impact of attentional deployment. For example, some experimental studies indicate that disengagement strategies, such as distraction and focus on external stimuli, can be associated with positive outcomes on pain intensity, toler-ance, and threshold (Nouwen et al., 2006; Rischer et al., 2020; Van Damme et al., 2008). In contrast, studies on pain-related fear also suggest that dis-engagement strategies can entail increased avoidance (Van Vliet et al., 2018; Zaman et al., 2015). On a similar note, while increased internal awareness has been suggested as an important process in mindfulness-based interventions (Gibson, 2019), excessive focus towards bodily sensa-tions in combination with threat-related interpretations has also been as-sociated with attentional bias towards pain and increased interference with activities (Broadbent et al., 2022; Todd et al., 2023). This brings me to the next section, highlighting the need to tailor treatments and adjust strate-gies to align with the goals, challenges, and context of the specific patient.
An Individualized and Tailored Approach
In studies examining cognitive behavioral therapies for chronic pain, several models propose that an individual's pre-treatment status can inter-act with the intervention, potentially moderating its effectiveness (Day et al., 2015; Vlaeyen & Crombez, 2020; Vlaeyen & Morley, 2005). For in-stance, Van Koulil et al. (2011) suggest that it might be important to con-sider behavioral patterns associated with pain persistence (e.g., persisting in activities and ignoring pain signals) and pain avoidance (e.g., fear of pain, catastrophizing, and hypervigilance). These behavioral patterns may require different treatment approaches since interventions targeting hy-pervigilance and avoidance may be counterproductive for patients persist-ing and ignoring pain.
On a similar note, a major challenge when selecting emotion regulation strategies to practice in treatment, is that outcomes of specific strategies often depend on the context (Linton et al., 2016). Hence, although it can be useful for clinicians to know what strategies often imply certain conse-quences, teaching ‘often functional’ strategies can be problematic if these are used in the wrong context (Gratz et al., 2015). For example, overt and covert avoidance behaviors, such as situation modification or distraction, are responses often targeted in exposure therapy since they predict poorer long-term outcomes of treatment (Weisman & Rodebaugh, 2018). These disengagement strategies could be conceptualized as dysfunctional in the
Emotion Regulation in Pain
38
context of therapy. However, avoidance behaviors when used in the right context can be important to prevent harm and increase self-efficacy (Hof-mann & Hay, 2018). Moreover, findings suggest that avoidance may not interfere with outcomes of exposure therapy when important information is not missed. Some authors have even proposed that temporary use of dis-traction and other avoidance behaviors could be beneficial for exposure in certain contexts, due to increased acceptability, tolerability, and increased self-efficacy (Weisman & Rodebaugh, 2018). Hence, it has been suggested that therapists should assess the function of avoidance behaviors before la-belling them as dysfunctional (Hofmann & Hay, 2018).
It has been argued that a detailed and comprehensive analysis of the individual is necessary to understand the underlying maintenance of a problem and how to initiate a change process (Hofmann & Hayes, 2019). In alignment with this proposition, several transdiagnostic approaches are individualized or tailored based on clinical case formulation (Schaeuffele et al., 2021). A tailored approach can imply difficulties when drawing con-clusions regarding the importance of specific interventions in trials due to increased treatment heterogeneity. However, given the diverse range of be-havioral patterns and comorbidities among patients, in addition to the eth-ical imperative to optimize and shorten treatments, I would suggest that relying on the therapist’s assessment of the patient might be the most use-ful available option. Better yet, the knowledge described in the introduction regarding transdiagnostic treatment processes could be combined with an individualized approach to tailor the treatment to patients’ specific needs.
The Hybrid Treatment
The hybrid emotion-focused exposure treatment, hereby referred to as the hybrid treatment, was developed for patients with comorbid pain and emotional distress (Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014). It integrates exposure meth-ods based on the fear-avoidance model of pain (Vlaeyen & Linton, 2012) with emotion regulation strategies from DBT (Koerner, 2012; Linehan & Wilks, 2015). Hence, the hybrid treatment target transdiagnostic pro-cesses, such as difficulties coping with emotional responses, as well as pain-related avoidance and catastrophizing. Furthermore, the manual empha-sizes the importance of tailoring interventions according to individual be-havioral patterns and goals, rather than relying on a fixed treatment plan (Linton & Klein-Strandberg, 2022).
Treatment Rationale
Linton & Fruzzetti (2014) developed the hybrid treatment since it was noted that exposure therapy for chronic pain, primarily focusing on fear of movements, could inadvertently neglect crucial emotional aspects among
Introduction
39
patients with comorbid emotional disorders. Failing to address these emo-tional aspects, and encouraging patients to engage in behaviors without ad-equately equipping them with the necessary skills to do so, was suggested to be potentially dismissive and invalidating. Therefore, an alternative ap-proach was recommended, allocating a significant amount of time to con-centrate on establishing goals, enhancing motivation, and training essen-tial regulation skills. The hybrid treatment manual emphasizes the im-portance of validation throughout the treatment, i.e., the therapist show-ing interest and modelling how to be self-compassionate and non-judg-mental (Fruzzetti & Ruork, 2019).
While it is problematized in the treatment manual that safety behaviors and disengagement strategies can hinder effects of exposure, it is also em-phasized that the primary goal is to enable the patient to engage with pre-viously avoided stimulus related to both pain and emotions. Hence, it is advised to tailor interventions in accordance with these treatment goals. The manual also underscores the importance of therapists working in col-laboration with patients as “avoidance detectives”. This approach involves validating the patient's experiences, while simultaneously helping them to recognize and reflect on the outcomes of dysfunctional avoidance behav-iors. Relevant behavioral patterns are assessed by using behavioral chain
analyses, i.e., a form of functional analysis, breaking down behaviors into a chain of events with situations, behavioral responses, and consequences (Linton & Klein-Strandberg, 2022).
Treatment Content
The hybrid treatment is presented in five stages, from focusing more on goal assessment, validation and building a working relationship, to-wards metaphors and skills training to prepare for exposure and behavioral experiments. Most strategies mentioned in the introduction are included in the brief overview of the hybrid treatment, presented in Table 1, using the terminology of the DBT literature (Linehan & Wilks, 2015; Lynch et al., 2006). Regarding emotion regulation skills, emphasis is put on acceptance and self-compassion, in accordance with mindfulness-based approaches (Shapiro et al., 2006; Wilson et al., 2019). In addition, the manual suggests training skills related to attentional deployment (e.g., refocusing and dis-
traction, and response modulation strategies including relaxation (e.g., re-fraining from unnecessary tensioning of muscles during movements) and opposite action (i.e., not letting emotions and thoughts dictate behavior). In the hybrid treatment metacognitive awareness and the dialectic stance is combined with behavioral experiments to investigate beliefs and possi-ble consequences of alternative behavioral patterns together with the pa-tient. Using behavioral experiments with the dialectic stance implies that
Emotion Regulation in Pain
40
alternative perspectives are constantly considered. Hence, rather than aim-ing at replacing one belief for another, the behavioral experiment is used to exemplify that our thoughts and perspectives seldom encompass the entire truth and does not have to guide our actions.
The treatment manual also encompasses valued commitment, an op-erant intervention that involves setting treatment goals aligned with what the patient identifies as personally meaningful and valuable. Metaphors
and psychoeducation are used to explain the principles of CBT to patients, and when confronted with obstacles to achieve goals the therapist would demonstrate methods for effective problem-solving. Additionally, one treatment stage is dedicated to training emotional disclosure (i.e., practic-ing how to communicate and disclose intimate feelings and experiences with others) and context sensitivity (i.e., learn how to identify relevant cues for when, where and with whom this might be beneficial). This stage was added to the manual after the initial feasibility study (Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014; Boersma et al., 2019; Linton & Klein-Strandberg, 2022). Table 1. A brief overview of the hybrid-emotion focused treatment (Boersma et al., 2019).
Treatment stage Typical methods
I. Building a working relation-ship, soothing distress, and developing relevant goals
Validation, self-monitoring and behav-ioral chain analyses, dialectic stance, metaphors and psychoeducation, goal setting, and valued commitment.
II. Developing skills to prepare for exposure and improve regulation of pain and emo-tion and everyday life
Psychoeducation, metaphors, dialectics, and skills training (self-validation, ac-ceptance, breathing and relaxation tech-niques, distraction, refocusing, problem-solving and opposite action).
III. Exposure for emotions and movements
Exposure in vivo, behavioral experi-ments generalize to home and work by practice.
IV. Training context sensitivity: applying skills in tune with environmental demands
Chain analysis and identifying relevant cues, rehearse context sensitive re-sponses, implementing validation, com-munication, and emotion-regulation skills, coping with responses from oth-ers.
V. Maintaining and refining Identifying key elements, strategies, and skills to cope with flare-ups.
Introduction
41
Feasibility of the Treatment
In the feasibility study by Linton & Fruzzetti (2014), six participants with pain and emotional distress provided ratings of pain intensity, physi-cal function, catastrophizing, acceptance, and negative affect at several time points before, during, and after the hybrid treatment. Compared to baseline, all participants showed clinically significant improvements on catastrophizing, acceptance, and negative affect post-treatment and at fol-low-up after 5 months. Moreover, five of six participants also improved on pain intensity and physical function. Hence, the authors concluded that combining emotion regulation skills training with exposure therapy could be a feasible approach to improve outcomes for patients with chronic pain and emotional distress.
What Works for Whom?
In addition to testing the efficacy of the hybrid treatment, it can be of importance to clarify how and when interventions change emotional re-sponses, investigate if these changes affect other outcomes, and try to iden-tify factors that can predict the effectiveness of a technique for a specific individual. In other words, it can be useful to understand the mediating
variables, or through which processes change occur, as well as moderating
variables, or under which circumstances changes occur. These approaches can also be combined to understand how mediators are moderated, or un-der which circumstances change occur through a specific process (Agler & De Boeck, 2017; Hayes & Rockwood, 2017; Morley & Keefe, 2007).
For instance, in accordance with the conceptual principles of the hybrid treatment, we suggest that improvements could be expected on emotion
regulation in general, or coping with emotional responses to any stimuli, probably effective on outcomes such as anxiety or symptoms of depression (Sloan et al., 2017). In addition, the treatment could have an impact on pain-related regulation, or coping with emotional responses to pain, prob-ably effective on pain interference, i.e., consequences of pain on relevant aspects of one’s life (Cederberg et al., 2016; Schemer et al., 2019; Smeets et al., 2006). Moreover, it is plausible that these effects are more salient among participants reporting larger difficulties with the same processes before treatment.
To further clarify what works, it can also be relevant to investigate the usefulness of specific emotion regulation strategies in different contexts. For instance, the hybrid treatment manual emphasizes several strategies from mindfulness-based approaches such as acceptance, self-compassion, refocusing, and a dialectical stance entailing metacognitive awareness. In addition, it is suggested in the manual that disengagement strategies, such as distraction, can be applied to reach relevant treatment goals (Linton &
Emotion Regulation in Pain
42
Fruzzetti, 2014; Linton & Klein-Strandberg, 2022). As previously noted in this introduction, it is challenging to provide clear insights into the impact and necessity of specific components such as engagement, disengagement, or attentional deployment in the context of mindfulness-based interven-tions. Consequently, clinicians may find it difficult to determine ideal tim-ing and suitability of these approaches without more knowledge on acute and long-term effects of specific strategies.
Overarching Aim This thesis primarily focuses on investigating possibilities to refine and
enhance CBT for chronic pain patients experiencing emotional distress by using emotion regulation strategies and skills training from mindfulness-based interventions.
Specific Aims of Empirical Studies
The aim of Study I was to evaluate the efficacy and acceptability of the hybrid treatment for chronic pain patients with clinical levels of emotional distress. To this end, the hybrid treatment was compared to an internet-delivered pain management treatment based on CBT principles (iCBT). Primary outcomes were pain intensity, pain interference, catastrophizing, anxiety, and symptoms of depression.
The aim of Study II was to investigate the importance of hypothesized treatment processes of the hybrid treatment, such as avoidance and emo-tion dysregulation, and if indirect effects were more pronounced for pa-tients who scored higher on these processes before treatment.
The aim of Study III was to gain knowledge that may contribute to our understanding of how similar interventions can be improved by evaluating the importance of attentional deployment in the context of mindfulness training. To this end, we investigated the impact of mindfulness exercises with internal or external focus of attention, when coping with experimen-tally induced pain.
Methods
43

##### METHODS

An Experimental Approach Experimental studies are crucial to establish causal connections and
gain further knowledge on how to improve interventions. Both randomized controlled trials (RCT’s) and experimental laboratory studies are im-
portant, serving somewhat different purposes in the research process. RCT’s are designed to test the efficacy of treatments. Experimental labora-tory studies focus on manipulating specific processes to examine their ef-fects, thereby offering valuable insights into the mechanisms of change as-sociated with specific interventions. While there is bi-directional inspira-tion between RCT’s and laboratory studies, a significant portion of treat-ments are not based on basic research findings. This indicates the need for a stronger link between different forms of experimental research (Ehring et al., 2022).
In this thesis, we employ both experimental approaches to investigate possibilities to enhance interventions for chronic pain patients experienc-ing emotional distress. Study I is an RCT examining the efficacy of the hy-brid treatment. In Study II we use mediation analysis on the same data to investigate indirect effects on outcomes. Lastly, Study III is a laboratory-based experiment, investigating acute effects of mindfulness exercises with different attentional focus on experiences of experimentally induced pain using the Cold Pressor Test (CPT). All studies use a randomized mixed ex-perimental design, considering differences both within subjects (i.e., before and after treatment or exercises) and between experimental conditions.
Participant Characteristics and Sample Size
Participants in Study I-II
Study I-II was a multicentre study involving 115 chronic pain patients recruited via advertisements in local newspapers, digital media, and reha-bilitation clinics.
Patients were eligible to the study if they had a) chronic musculoskele-tal pain (>6 months); b) functional problems in daily life due to pain; c) emotional problems (anxiety or depression); and d) access to computer or tablet; and e) sufficient mastery of the Swedish language. Exclusion criteria were a) pain emanating from malignancies, systemic diseases, or localized single-joint osteoarthritic conditions in the lower extremities; b) severe
Emotion Regulation in Pain
44
psychiatric disorders that required other treatment; c) ongoing psycholog-ical treatment elsewhere; or d) recently started or changed psychopharma-cological treatment (<3 months prior to planned treatment start).
The study sample, presented in Table 2, primarily consisted of middle-aged individuals, predominantly female (83%), experiencing pain in mul-tiple areas for several years. In accordance with inclusion criteria, all par-ticipants reported symptoms of anxiety and depression. Approximately two-thirds of the sample met the clinical criteria for an anxiety or depres-sive disorder according to the Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Inter-view (Sheehan et al., 1998). Participants in Study III
Study III was an experimental study involving 204 healthy adults re-cruited via local and digital media advertisements. Individuals were eligible if they were 18-65 years old and reported a) no current chronic or acute pain, psychiatric disorder, large scar or tissue damage on the dominant hand or arm, and uncorrected hearing loss or visual impairment; b) no his-tory of cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, Reynaud’s disease, or
Methods
45
cold injuries; c) no recent use of alcohol or analgesics; and d) good under-standing of the Swedish language. Participants were allocated using block randomization with a random block size of 3 or 6, and stratified by sex to ensure a balanced sample across conditions.
The study sample, presented in Table 3, was predominantly female (71%) and reported average levels of mindfulness skills (Lilja et al., 2020), high preference for reappraisal strategies (Enebrink et al., 2013; Spaapen et al., 2014), and high levels of pain-related anxiety (Abrams et al., 2007; Wallin et al., 2012) compared to other healthy populations.
