Experimental Conditions
Experimental Conditions in Study I-II
The Hybrid Treatment
The hybrid treatment included 10-15 weekly sessions conducted by five licensed clinical psychologists, and two psychologists in their post-gradu-ate year of supervised professional training. Therapists were provided with the treatment manual (Linton & Klein-Strandberg, 2022), including de-scriptions of goals for each treatment stage, as well as suggestions on meth-ods and materials for exercises. For a brief overview of treatment content, consult Table 1 in the subsection on the hybrid treatment in the introduc-tion.
In accordance with the tailored approach suggested by the treatment manual, therapists were not provided with specific session content, amount
Emotion Regulation in Pain
46
of treatment sessions per stage, or precise step-by-step guidance. Thera-pists received training, supervision, and filled out checklists on methods used and homework assigned for each session.
Treatments lasted for median (IQR) 17.5 (16-21) weeks, and median (IQR) 12.6 (7.9-19.4) hours per treatment. At the start of treatment, thera-pists assessed emotional disorders with the Mini International Neuropsy-chiatric Interview (MINI). In addition, before exposure for movements, participants were examined by a physiotherapist. If there were uncertain-ties or concerns regarding the appropriateness of certain movements, a senior specialist in rehabilitation medicine was consulted.
The Internet-Delivered Pain Management Treatment
The internet-delivered pain management treatment based on CBT principles (iCBT), included eight treatment modules guided by two li-censed clinical psychologists, two psychologists in their post-graduate year of supervised professional training, and four psychology students in their final stage of clinical training. The treatment consisted of psychoeducation, exercises, and homework assignments provided in text with pictures and audio files. For a brief overview of the treatment content see Buhrman et al. (2004), and table 3 in Boersma et al. (2019).
Before the treatment started, the therapist contacted the patient over telephone to conduct a pain assessment interview and the MINI. Further communication was conducted over the internet platform when needed, with patients receiving responses from the therapist within 24 hours on working days.
Experimental Conditions in Study II
The Cold Pressor Test
The Cold Pressor Test (CPT) is a thermal stimulation that involves im-mersion of the forearm, hand, or other extremity in ice cold water, provid-ing noxious cooling. It is a commonly used method to study effects on ex-perimentally induced pain of mindfulness exercises (Liu et al., 2013; Petter et al., 2013, 2014) and acceptance training (Kohl et al., 2012).
All participants in Study III underwent the same CPT twice, before and after experimental conditions. The test involved instructions to submerge the dominant hand in a container with lukewarm water (36±1°C) for 2 minutes, and subsequently submerge the same hand in a container with circulating cold water (5°C). Participants were instructed to say “now” if
they started to perceive the experience as painful and try to keep their hand in the cold water for as long as it was tolerable. Participants still holding
Methods
47
their hand in the cold water after 5 minutes were instructed to remove it. However, they were not informed of this time limit beforehand.
All instructions were pre-recorded and presented to participants over wireless headphones with active noise-reduction, together with accompa-nying text and illustrations presented on a computer screen. To ensure a uniform auditory environment, all participants were exposed to the same recorded ambient sounds during the CPT.
Mindfulness Exercises
Both mindfulness exercises included a brief rationale to increase non-judgmental metacognitive awareness, and a 12-minute training of atten-tional control by directing attention towards different body parts (internal focus condition), or different sounds and sound locations (external focus condition). The mindfulness rationale was based on acceptance training protocols used in earlier studies (Forsyth & Hayes, 2014; Keogh et al., 2005; Masedo & Esteve, 2007; Wang et al., 2019) with psychoeducation on acceptance, metacognitive awareness, and mindfulness-based response modulation, as well as an instruction to have an open and accepting atti-tude towards negative thoughts or feelings during the upcoming CPT.
The 12-minute audio exercise for attention training in the internal fo-
cus condition was based on the body scan meditation (Dreeben et al., 2013; Kabat-Zinn, 1982). Initially, participants received instructions to keep their focus for extended periods on regions of their dominant hand and arm. Gradually, they were directed to increase the frequency of switching their focus, encompassing their entire body, and ending on their left foot (35 body parts in total). Finally, participants were guided to expand their at-tention, starting with focusing on two locations simultaneously, and finally being aware of their whole body, with a flexible and freely shifting focus.
In the external focus condition, a modified version of the same record-ing was used with instructions to focus on different sounds and spatial lo-cations (near and far away or to the left and right), while listening to a soundscape consisting of wind chimes, flying bumblebees, crickets chirp-ing, running water, birds singing, owls howling, and passing cars. The sounds were carefully selected and adjusted during pilots to ensure that fo-cusing on sounds was relatively easy, and a pleasant experience for most participants. Since the body scan in the internal focus condition included more body parts than available sounds, participants in the external focus condition began switching back and forth between sounds and locations. As in the internal focus condition, participants were guided to expand their attention gradually, finally broadening their attention towards the full soundscape, with a flexible and freely shifting focus.
Emotion Regulation in Pain
48
Spontaneous Coping
In the spontaneous coping condition, participants listened to a scien-tific podcast about archaeology for the same duration as the combined time of the mindfulness rationale and exercises (22 minutes). These participants received no instructions or information on strategies to use during the up-coming CPT.

Pain Measures
One-Dimensional Measures
The CPT allows participants to exercise control over when to report the experience as being painful, and when to remove their hand from the cold water. These behavioral responses can be observed and timed to provide quantitative data. Pain threshold is defined as the time interval from when participants submerge their hands into the cold water until they report that they experience pain. Pain tolerance is defined as the time interval from submersion of the hand in the cold water until removal (von Baeyer et al., 2005). These measures were used as primary outcomes in Study III.
In addition, participants in Study III rated pain intensity during the CPT from “no pain” (0) to “extremely intense pain” (10), pain unpleasant-
ness from “not unpleasant” (0) to “extremely unpleasant” (10), level of dis-
tress provoked by the task from “no distress” (0) to “extremely intense dis-tress” (10), and how often they had negative thoughts about their experi-ences during the CPT from “not at all” (0) to “all the time” (10).
Multi-Dimensional Pain Assessment
The West Haven-Yale Multidimensional Pain Inventory, MPI (Kerns et al., 1985), is rooted in behavioral and cognitive behavioral theories and as-sess psychosocial and behavioral consequences of pain.
In Study I and II, we use two subscales from the MPI-S as outcome measures. The MPI-pain intensity subscale consists of two items rated on 6-point scales regarding pain in the present moment from “no pain” (0) to “very intense pain” (6), and pain for the last week from “not at all severe” (0) to “extremely severe” (6). Total scores range from 0-12. The MPI-pain
interference subscale consists of 11 items rated on 6-point scales from 0-6, with unique anchors for each item. Total scores range from 0-66. Both sub-scales have demonstrated acceptable to good test-retest reliability in a Swe-dish sample, r=.75 for pain intensity and r=.85 for pain interference (Berg-strom et al., 1999).
Symptoms of Depression and Anxiety
The Montgomery Åsberg Depression Rating Scale – Self report (MADRS-S) assessing symptoms of depression (Fantino & Moore, 2009; Zimmerman et al., 2004) was used in Study I and II as a primary outcome measure. It is a frequently used scale that has shown high sensitivity and specificity compared to more extensive diagnostic instruments among Swe-dish primary care patients with depression (Nejati et al., 2020). MADRS-S consists of 9 items rated on 6-point scales from 0-6, with unique anchors for each item. Total scores range from 0-60. It has shown acceptable test-
Emotion Regulation in Pain
50
retest reliability, r = .78 (Fantino & Moore, 2009), and was translated and validated in a Swedish sample by (Svanborg & Asberg, 2001).
The Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item Scale (GAD-7) was used in Study I as an outcome measure. It was developed to assess symptoms of GAD (Spitzer et al., 2006), but has also been recommended as a tool to as-sess symptoms of anxiety related to several disorders in primary care (Kroenke et al., 2007; Plummer et al., 2016). GAD-7 consists of 7 items re-garding symptoms of anxiety and participants rate on a 4-point scale how often they were bothered by each symptom during the last 14 days from “not at all” (0) to “nearly every day” (3). Total scores range from 0-27. It has shown good test-retest reliability, r = .83 (Spitzer et al., 2006), and has been translated and previously used in Swedish samples (Johansson et al., 2013; Rozental et al., 2014).
General Emotion Regulation
The Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS) is an acceptance-based measure of emotion dysregulation (Gratz & Roemer, 2004) that has been found to be associated with outcomes of acceptance and mindfulness-based interventions (Gratz & Tull, 2010). It was used in the latent variable general emotion dysregulation in Study II. DERS consists of 36 items re-garding levels of emotion dysregulation across six domains; non-ac-ceptance of negative emotions, inability to engage in goal-directed behav-iors when distressed, difficulties controlling impulsive behaviors when dis-tressed, limited access to effective emotion regulation strategies, lack of emotional awareness, and lack of emotional clarity. Participants rate the extent to which each item applies to them on a 5-point scale, ranging from “almost never” (1) to “almost always” (5). Total scores range from 36 to 180. DERS has demonstrated good test-retest reliability, r=.88 (Gratz & Roe-mer, 2004), and it was translated and validated in a Swedish sample by Bjureberg et al., (2016).
The Self-Compassion Scale-12 (SCS-12), assessing emotion regulation strategies such as cognitive reappraisal, self-compassion, and acceptance (Raes et al., 2011), was used in the latent variable general emotion dysreg-
ulation in Study II. SCS-12 consists of 12 items, and participants rate the extent to which each item applies to them on a 5-point scale ranging from “almost never” (1) to “almost always” (5). Total scores range from 12-60. It has demonstrated good test-retest reliability, r=.89 (Garcia-Campayo et al., 2014), and was translated and validated in a Swedish sample by (Bratt & Fagerstrom, 2019).
The Behavioral Activation for Depression Scale (BADS), assessing dif-ficulties with goal pursuit, avoidance behaviors, social withdrawal, and ru-
Methods
51
mination (Kanter et al., 2007), was used in the latent variable general emo-
tion dysregulation in Study II. BADS consists of 25 statements and partic-ipants rate the extent to which each statement was true to them during the last week on a 7-point scale from “not at all” (0) to “completely” (6). Total scores range from 0-150. It has demonstrated acceptable test-retest relia-bility, r=.74 (Kanter et al., 2007) and was translated and validated in a Swe-dish sample by Björstad & Johansson (2008).
The Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ), assessing general emo-tion regulation strategies (Gross & John, 2003), was used for sample char-
acterization in Study III. ERQ consists of 10 statements regarding two sub-scales, use of cognitive reappraisal (6 items, average score 1-7) and expres-sive suppression (4 items, average score 1-7). Participants rate how much they agree with each statement on a 7-point scale ranging from “strongly disagree” (1) to “strongly agree” (7). It was translated and validated in a Swedish sample by Enebrink et al. (2013).
The Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ), assessing use of mindfulness strategies such as observing, describing, acting with aware-ness, non-judging, and non-reactivity to inner experiences (Baer et al., 2008), was used for sample characterization in Study III. FFMQ consists of 29 statements regarding the use of strategies and participants rate how often they apply these on a 5-point scale from “never” (1) to “always” (5). Total average ranges from 1-5. It has been translated and validated in a Swedish sample by Lilja et al. (2011).
Pain-Related Dysregulation
The Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), assessing negative thinking re-lated to actual or anticipated pain experiences (Sullivan et al., 1995), was used as an outcome measure in Study I, and in the latent variable pain-
related dysregulation in Study II. PCS consists of 13 items reflecting thoughts and feelings that individuals may experience when they are in pain. Respondents are asked to rate the extent to which they have these thoughts and feelings on a five-point scale, ranging from “not at all” (0) to “all the time” (4). Total scores range from 0-52. It has demonstrated ac-ceptable test-retest reliability, r=.75 (Sullivan et al., 1995), and has been translated, previously used, and validated in Swedish samples (Buer & Lin-ton, 2002; Flink et al., 2010; Karlsson & Linderoth, 2018). The Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia-11 (TSK-11), assessing fear of re-injury or worsening of pain due to movements and activities (Woby et al., 2005), was used in the latent variable pain-related dysregulation in Study
II. TSK-11 consists of 11 items and participants rate how much they agree with each statement on a 4-point scale ranging from “strongly disagree” (1) to “strongly agree” (4). Total scores range from 11-44. It has demonstrated
Emotion Regulation in Pain
52
good test-retest reliability, r=.81 (Hapidou et al., 2012), and has been trans-lated and validated a Swedish sample (Roelofs et al., 2007).
The short version of the Chronic Pain Acceptance Questionnaire (CPAQ-8), assessing the ability to engage in activities in the presence of pain and willingness to experience pain (Fish et al., 2010), was used in the latent variable pain-related dysregulation in Study II. CPAQ-8 consists of 8 statements and participants rate how much they believe these to be true on a 7-point scale from “never true” (0) to “always true” (6). Total scores range from 0-48. It has been translated and validated in a Swedish sample (Rovner et al., 2014).
The short version of the Pain Anxiety Symptoms Scale (PASS-20), as-sessing pain-related fear, escape/avoidance strategies, negative thinking and physiological symptoms of anxiety when confronting pain (McCracken & Dhingra, 2002), was used for sample characterization in Study III. PASS-20 consists of 20 statements and participants rate how often these are true to them on a 6-point scale from “never” (0) to “always” (5). It has been translated and previously used in Swedish samples (Wallin et al., 2012).
State Emotion Regulation
The State Emotion Regulation Inventory (SERI) measure the use of distraction, reappraisal, rumination, and acceptance strategies (Katz et al., 2017). In study III we used a modified version of three subscales: distrac-
tion (4 statements, average 1-7), reappraisal (4 statements, average 1-7) and acceptance (4 statements, average 1-7). Participants rated how much they agreed with each statement on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from “to-tally disagree” (1) to “totally agree” (7). The 12 statements were translated into Swedish, and the instructions were modified to clarify that they re-ferred to experiences during the latest CPT.
In Study III, participants were asked to rate, on a scale from “not at all” (0) to “completely” (10), the extent to which they believed their thoughts reflected a true or accurate description of reality, their level of awareness of their thinking, and the degree to which they approached their experi-ences with acceptance and openness during the second CPT. Additionally, participants rated their willingness to engage in the CPT for a third time, using a scale ranging from “not at all” (0) to “very willing” (10).
Attentional Focus
To assess attentional focus during CPT, participants in Study III were asked to rate the frequency of attentional focus during CPT towards differ-ent areas of the body, sounds, thoughts, and visual stimuli. They provided
Methods
53
ratings on a scale ranging from “not at all focused” (0) to “completely fo-cused on this all the time” (10). To aid in this assessment, we employed an illustration of a human body inspired by manikins commonly used to eval-uate pain sensations (Jones et al., 2013; Novembre et al., 2019).
To assess the direction of attentional focus (i.e., whether it was pre-dominantly internal or external) before and after mindfulness exercises in Study III, we used the 7-point numerical Likert scale by Wells (2009). The scale ranges from “entirely focused on surroundings” (-3) to “entirely fo-cused on self” (+3). Previous studies have demonstrated significant effects on this measure of attention training focused on external stimuli compared to internally focused mindfulness exercises (Fergus et al., 2014), and relax-ation training (Sharpe et al., 2010). To facilitate interpretability, we con-verted the scores to a 0 to 6 scale, where a score of 6 represents being en-tirely focused on the surroundings.
Treatment Acceptability
Treatment acceptability was assessed in Study I at mid-treatment us-ing 3 questions of the Credibility/Expectancy Questionnaire (Devilly & Borkovec, 2000) regarding if their treatment was logical for them, could be successful, and if they would recommend it to a friend, on a numerical rat-ing scale from 0 to 10. To assess treatment satisfaction and global im-
provement post-treatment, participants were asked to rate how pleased they were with the treatment, if they would recommend it to someone with similar difficulties, positive effects of the treatment on their ability to cope with pain, and well-being, on a numerical rating scale from 0 to 5. Both scales had unique anchors for each item. In addition, participants were asked to report if any adverse events had occurred, provide specifics in free text, and estimate how much this affected their well-being during the past week from “not at all” (0) to “very much” (6).
Statistical Analyses Various software packages were utilized for the statistical analyses con-
ducted in Study I-III. Specifically, SPSS (Version 24) was employed for de-scriptive statistics and the analysis of simple associations in Study I. Mplus was utilized for primary outcome analyses in Study I (Version 8.1) and structural equation modelling in Study II (Version 8.2). Additionally, R Statistical Software (Version 4.3.0) was utilized for descriptive statistics, effect size calculations, and robust regression models in Study III.
Throughout, comparisons were two-tailed and treated as statistically significant at the level of p < .05. Confidence intervals are given with 95% margin (95% CI).
Emotion Regulation in Pain
54
In Study I, a combination of basic parametric and non-parametric sta-tistical methods was utilized to analyse treatment acceptability measures and simple associations between adherence and outcomes. Parametric tests such as t-test and analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used for contin-uous variables when underlying assumptions were met, and non-paramet-ric tests such as Mann-Whitney U test and chi-square tests were used when we needed to rely on ranks or orderings of data.
Robust Models
In Study I, the primary analytic model for testing the differences be-tween the hybrid treatment and iCBT involved regression analyses for both continuous and categorical outcome variables. These analyses were con-ducted using maximum likelihood estimation with non-normality robust standard errors, which were obtained through the MLR option in Mplus (Muthén et al., 2016; Muthén & Muthén, 2017). The difference between treatments was tested using the treatment variable (0.5 = hybrid treatment, -0.5 = iCBT) and the pre-treatment values of the outcome variable (grand mean centred) as predictors, similar to analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). This is approach was preferred over simple analysis of raw change scores, since it produces more reliable and unbiased estimates in most circum-stances (Senn, 2006).
In Study II, data models were estimated within the framework of struc-tural equation modelling (SEM) and fitted with full information maximum likelihood estimation and non-normality robust standard errors (MLR or Bootstrap) using Mplus (Muthén & Muthén, 2017). These statistical meth-ods are discussed in greater detail in the section of the text dedicated to mediation analyses.
In Study III, the primary analytic model for testing the differences be-tween conditions on continuous outcomes was a series of robust regression models based on an M-estimator using iteratively reweighted least squares (IRWLS) estimation (Koller & Stahel, 2017). We used orthogonal contrasts to examine the difference between mindfulness exercises and spontaneous coping (0.33 = external focus, 0.33 = internal focus, -0.66 = spontaneous coping), and external and internal focus conditions (0.5 = external focus, -0.5 = internal focus). Additionally, we included covariates such as sex and baseline values when appropriate, to account for their potential influence on the outcomes. Robust regression models were calculated using the ro-bustbase package v0.95-1 in R (Maechler et al., 2021).
Methods
55
Calculating Effect Sizes
In Study I and III, we primarily used standardized mean differences (Cohen's d) as effect size measures. Since the accuracy of Cohen’s d relies
on assumptions on normality and homogeneity of variances (Cohen, 2013; Li, 2016), we aimed to obtain more reliable effect sizes by using estimates, adjusted means, and variances derived from the robust regression models.
In Study I, we calculated a non-robust within-group Cohen’s d for de-scriptive purposes, using the pooled standard deviation at pre-treatment as the denominator (Becker, 1988). For between-group comparisons, we used model implied (adjusted) means and variances for continuous variables, and the standard deviation at pre-treatment as the denominator. To assess categorical outcomes, we computed the odds ratio as a standardized effect size measure based on model estimates (Haddock et al., 1998).
In Study III, we calculated an estimate of Cohen's d from t-test values, group sample sizes, multiple correlation, and the number of covariates from robust regression models (Borenstein, 2009) using the compute.es package v0.2-5 in R (Del Re, 2013).
Consistent with guidelines by Cohen (2013), effect sizes of 0.2 to 0.5 were considered small, 0.5 to 0.8 moderate, and values equal to or greater than 0.8 were considered large.
Reliable and Clinically Significant Change
To assess clinically significant changes in Study I, we employed the cri-teria proposed by Jacobson et al. (1999). To determine if the observed changes were beyond what could be expected due to measurement error alone, the reliable change index (RCI) was calculated using the pooled standard deviation of the observed sample at baseline, and the test-retest reliability of the measures. For clinical significance, we considered whether the observed changes met the criteria for reliable improvement based on the RCI. Additionally, we evaluated recovery, which was defined as a score shifting from a clinical range to a non-clinical range. In other words, clini-
cally significant improvement is defined as a reliable improvement plac-ing the individual closer to the mean of the functional population than the mean of the dysfunctional population (Jacobson et al., 1999).
The specific cut-off values for recovery were determined based on rec-ommended thresholds for highest possible specificity and sensitivity in identifying clinical and non-clinical cases. For the MADRS-S measure, we used a cut-off value of 9 (Zimmerman et al., 2004). For the GAD-7, we used a cut-off value of 10 (Spitzer et al., 2006). For the PCS, the cut-off value was set as the midpoint between the distributions of catastrophizers and non-catastrophizers, 21 (Sullivan et al., 1995). For the MPI subscales, values ly-ing two standard deviations below the mean in our baseline sample were
Emotion Regulation in Pain
56
used. Specifically, a cut-off value of 2.98 was used for pain intensity, and a value of 26.63 was used for pain interference. Subsequently, reliable im-
provement and clinically significant improvement were analysed as two categorical outcome variables (1 = improvement, 0 = no improvement) in the primary outcome analyses.
Mediation Analysis
In Study I-II, we utilized several measures that were chosen to capture suggested mediators. However, when analysing mediation in that context, it becomes crucial to employ a method that consider the overlap among measures. This is important both from a theoretical perspective, ensuring the validity of our findings, and from a methodological perspective, ensur-ing the accuracy of our statistical analysis (Cheung & Lau, 2007; Holmbeck, 1997). One suggested approach, that we applied in Study II, is to decrease the amount of overlapping observed variables to a smaller set of latent di-mensions, commonly referred to as latent variables, using SEM (Cheung & Lau, 2015; Muthén & Asparouhov, 2014).
For the latent variable of pain-related dysregulation, we used the total scores on PCS, TSK-11, and CPAQ-8. These instruments assess various cog-nitive-behavioral processes specific to pain. Although each measure is as-sociated with slightly different theoretical perspectives, they share com-monalities and overlap in their conceptualization. Specifically, they all rec-ognize that pain can elicit emotional responses and involve cognitive and behavioral efforts to control and avoid pain (Fish et al., 2010; Flink et al., 2013; Hapidou et al., 2012).
For the latent variable of general emotion dysregulation, we used the total scores on DERS, SCS-12, and BADS. These instruments focus on cog-nitive and behavioral strategies employed to regulate emotional responses in different contexts (Gratz & Roemer, 2004; Kanter et al., 2007; Raes et al., 2011). To ensure consistency and interpretability, we transformed the CPAQ-8, SCS-12, and BADS scores prior to conducting the analyses. This transformation was done to ensure that all factor loadings were positive, meaning that higher scores would indicate greater dysfunction.
Figure 2 summarize the suggested moderated mediation model of the hybrid treatment, with improved emotion regulation as a mediator.

Figure 2. Theoretical model of moderated mediation of the hybrid treatment on pain interference and emotional distress. Effects of suggested interventions on mediators (a-path), effect of mediator on outcomes (b-path), indirect effects of interventions on outcomes through mediator (ab-product), direct effects of inter-ventions on outcomes without change on the mediator (c-path), and effects of potential moderators on a-paths.
Testing the Adequacy of the Model We employed several procedures to evaluate the adequacy of our pro-
posed latent variables and two-factor structure, including Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) at each time point, and in a combined longitudinal CFA model. This allowed us to examine the facture structure across both time points and assess the stability and consistency over time (Little, 2013). The goodness of fit of our models was evaluated using multiple fit indices, such as chi-square tests, the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation, the Comparative Fit Index, and the Standardized Root Mean Square Resid-ual (Bentler, 1990; Hu & Bentler, 1999; J. Wang & Wang, 2012).
To examine longitudinal measurement invariance (i.e., if measurement properties remain persistent over time for each latent variable), intercepts and factor loadings were constrained to be equal across different measure points (Little, 2013; Wickrama et al., 2016). This model was compared to a configural model, in which constraints were removed (Muthén & Muthén, 2017; Satorra & Bentler, 2001).

Testing for Mediation
To test for mediation, the latent variables were used as mediators in a path model. This involved using regression analysis to examine associa-tions between treatment condition (X), the latent variables measured at post-treatment (M), and the observed outcomes of depression and pain in-terference assessed at the 9-month follow-up (Y). Specifically, we regressed the latent mediator variables measured at post-treatment on the treatment condition (a-path), which was represented as a binary coded variable (1 = hybrid treatment, 0 = iCBT). Additionally, we regressed the observed out-come at the 9-month follow-up on the latent mediator (b-path). To account for baseline scores on both the observed outcome and the latent mediator, the mediator and outcome measured at post-treatment and follow-up, were regressed on pre-treatment assessments (similar to an ANCOVA model).
To evaluate mediation, we used bootstrapping to estimate confidence intervals around the product of the a- and b-paths, commonly referred to as the ab-product (MacKinnon et al., 2007). Bootstrapping involves draw-ing repeated samples with replacement from the dataset (in this case 5000 samples), allowing us to estimate the distribution of the ab-product under different resampling scenarios. By constructing these bootstrapped confi-dence intervals, we obtained a robust estimate of the indirect effect and its variability. If the 95% CI around the ab-product did not include zero, it in-dicated that mediation was established at the specified alpha level (.05).
Testing for Moderated Mediation
To test the influence of pre-treatment levels on mediators, also known as mediated baseline by treatment moderation (MacKinnon et al., 2007; Preacher et al., 2007), an interaction term was created by multiplying the pre-treatment measurement of the latent variable with the treatment con-dition variable. Subsequently, to evaluate moderated mediation, we as-sessed whether the product of the regression coefficients representing the interaction effect (moderated a-path) and the association between the me-diator and outcome (b-path) significantly differed from zero. Similar to the mediation assessment, we utilized bootstrapping to estimate a 95% asym-metric CI around the product of the regression coefficients. If the confi-dence interval did not span zero, it indicated the presence of moderated mediation. To further understand the significance and size of the effect, as recommended for moderated mediation analysis (Preacher et al., 2007), we examined conditional indirect effects on the outcome, from two stand-ard deviations above to two standard deviations below the mean of the moderator variable.
Methods
59
Ethical Considerations Psychological interventions often require participants to confront and
manage discomfort, to develop skills in handling unpleasant emotions and experiences. Consequently, it is crucial to consider and address the ethical implications and potential risks associated with conducting such a study. It is worth noting that previous studies regarding similar treatments (Bo-ersma et al., 2004; Linton et al., 2008; Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014) have not reported any significant negative experiences among participants. None-theless, to ensure the well-being of our participants, we took proactive measures by assembling a research team consisting of experienced psy-chologists who possess the expertise to effectively manage and address po-tential adverse effects. Moreover, concerns raised by participants were promptly responded to, and documented. Participants in all studies were informed about the objectives, procedures, potential risks, and benefits be-fore voluntarily agreeing to participate by written consent.
Survey questions regarding pain experiences, emotion regulation, and psychological well-being, may potentially be perceived as uncomfortable or intrusive. However, no significant issues of that nature have been reported regarding the standardized questionnaires used in these studies. Further-more, all participants had access to names and email addresses of the re-searchers, allowing them to provide feedback on the questions if desired.
In Study I-II, the benefits were likely to be relatively significant for the participants involved. All participants received an active treatment led by psychologists, and previous research have shown that both methods used in the project can have positive effects for patients with chronic pain (Buhr-man et al., 2004, 2011; Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014). Therefore, it could not be predetermined whether the control treatment was anything other than an equivalent alternative to the hybrid treatment. Participants in Study I-II were informed about the randomization process and the treatment options. They were also informed that they could withdraw from the study at any time, and that their participation did not affect access to regular healthcare.
Regarding Study III, the benefit for research participants was regarded as limited, thus warranting financial compensation for their participation. In addition, the CPT is expected to involve temporary discomfort, and can be perceived as painful by many individuals. However, the CPT is consid-ered safe, and does not have any long-term physical or psychological nega-tive consequences for individuals who meet the inclusion criteria (Von Bae-yer et al., 2005). All participants were clearly informed about the tempo-rary discomfort that the CPT may entail. They were also informed that they had the option to immediately withdraw and end their participation at any point during the experiment, without the need to provide a reason, and
Emotion Regulation in Pain
60
without facing any negative consequences. To minimize the risk of partici-pants continuing with the experiment despite high levels of discomfort due to economic incentives, participants were informed that compensation would be provided before the start of the experiment.
In a broader perspective, these studies were not considered to have any significant negative ethical implications. The potential benefits of address-ing the research questions were deemed to outweigh temporary discomfort and potential risks for participants, especially considering the measures taken to minimize them. The studies could provide valuable knowledge about the interaction between pain, emotions, and emotion regulation, contributing to new hypotheses regarding undiscovered treatment mecha-nisms in psychological interventions for patients with chronic pain. More-over, the findings may also contribute to the refinement of theories of emo-tion regulation in a broader sense, entailing implications for interventions in various psychiatric disorders.
All studies were approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (Dnr 2015/479 for Study I-II, and Dnr 2021-00256 for Study III).

Results
61

##### RESULTS

Study I: Efficacy of a Transdiagnostic Treatment The results of Study I presented in Figure 3, suggest that the hybrid
treatment was more effective than iCBT post-treatment on pain interfer-ence (p<.001, d=0.63) and pain catastrophizing (p<.01, d=0.39); and at follow-up on pain interference (p=.02, d=0.51) and symptoms of depres-sion (p=.04, d=0.43). Regarding general anxiety, pain intensity, and pro-portions of reliable and clinically significant improvements, we found no significant differences between treatments.
Figure 3. Effect sizes of the hybrid treatment vs iCBT on primary outcome measures (a) post-treatment, and (b) at 9-month follow-up. Effect sizes were cal-culated using model implied means and variance, with the SD at pre-treatment as the denominator.
Within-group effect sizes for the hybrid treatment at follow-up were large on symptoms of depression (d=1.13), general anxiety (d=.84), pain catastrophizing (d=.97), and pain interference (d=1.17); and small on pain intensity (d=.40). Within-group effect sizes for iCBT at follow-up were moderate on all outcomes (d=.65-.73). Approximately 20-24% receiving the hybrid treatment, and 8-16% receiving iCBT, reported clinically signif-icant improvements in all outcomes except pain intensity, where very few reported improvements regardless of treatment (2-4%). 72% receiving the

hybrid treatment, and 56% receiving iCBT, reported reliable improvements on at least one outcome measure at follow-up. These improvements were clinically significant for 52% receiving the hybrid treatment, and 35% re-ceiving iCBT. Observed differences in proportions between treatments were not significant.
The hybrid treatment was well accepted, with participants reporting higher treatment credibility (p=.001), treatment satisfaction (p<.001), and global impression of improvement (p=.001) compared to iCBT. Differences regarding reported adverse events was not significant. The most reported adverse events were increased symptoms of depression or anxiety (3 par-ticipants in the hybrid treatment), and stress due to homework assign-ments (6 participants receiving iCBT). Of the 115 participants, 78% com-pleted assessments post-treatment and 82% at follow-up. Missing data was not related to treatment allocation, but higher anxiety in the iCBT group increased the likelihood of missing data at post-treatment (p=.03), and at follow-up (p=.01). No other variables were related to non-participation. There were differences in the degree of adherence, where participants in the hybrid treatment completed a larger portion of the recommended con-tent (p<.001). However, this did not relate to effects on primary outcomes.
Study II: Processes of Change The results of Study II, presented in Figure 4, suggest that the hybrid
treatment had a stronger impact than iCBT on both mediators (a-paths). In addition, both mediators had a significant impact on outcomes (b-paths). Specifically, decreased pain-related dysregulation mediated effects of treat-ment on pain interference and symptoms of depression, and improved gen-eral emotion dysregulation mediated effects on symptoms of depression.
In addition, we found partial support for the hypothesis that indirect effects were moderated by pre-treatment levels on the mediators. Specifi-cally, individuals with higher scores on pain-related dysregulation reported a more pronounced change on this mediator compared to those scoring lower (β=−0.479, p=.012), thereby moderating indirect effects on pain in-terference (β−3.285, 95% CI [−7.081, −0.298]) and symptoms of depres-sion (β=−3.052, 95% CI [−6.232, −0.621]).
The fit indices provided evidence of a good fit between our models and the data. Furthermore, all factor loadings for the indicators were found to be notably high, supporting the use of latent variables. Additionally, tests of longitudinal measure invariance indicated that imposing constraints on factor loadings and intercepts had no detrimental effect on the overall model fit.

cus on the hand submerged in the cold water compared to spontaneous coping (p=.002, d =-0.46). In accordance with experimental manipulation, participants in the external focus condition, compared to the internal focus, reported being more focused on the surroundings directly after the exercise (p <.0001, d =1.93), along with more focus towards sounds (p=.029, d =0.37), and less focus on other body parts (p<.001, d =-0.62), during the subsequent CPT.
