##### 

Discussion
67

##### DISCUSSION

The overarching aim of this thesis was to investigate possibilities to en-
hance CBT for chronic pain patients experiencing emotional distress, by using emotion regulation strategies and skills training from mindfulness-based interventions.
In Study I we evaluated the efficacy and acceptability of the hybrid treatment, integrating exposure therapy with emotion regulation strategies from DBT, for patients with chronic pain and clinical levels of emotional distress. We found that the hybrid treatment was more effective than the active control condition (iCBT) on pain interference and pain catastrophiz-ing post-treatment, and on pain interference and symptoms of depression at 9-month follow-up. In addition, participants receiving the hybrid treat-ment reported higher treatment credibility, satisfaction, and global impres-sion of improvement.
In Study II we investigated if improved emotion regulation post-treat-ment mediated effects of the hybrid treatment compared to iCBT on out-comes at 9-month follow-up. Measures related to emotion regulation were used as indicators for two latent variables: pain-related dysregulation (catastrophizing, fear-avoidance, and non-acceptance of pain), and general
emotion dysregulation (difficulties to regulate a wider range of emotional responses). The analysis revealed that decreased pain-related dysregula-tion mediated the effects of the hybrid treatment compared to iCBT on both pain interference and symptoms of depression. Furthermore, indirect ef-fects through pain-related dysregulation were more evident for partici-pants scoring higher on this variable at baseline. In addition, decreased general emotion dysregulation mediated effects of the hybrid treatment compared to iCBT on symptoms of depression.
In Study III we investigated the impact of mindfulness exercises with different attentional focus when coping with experimentally induced pain. Our findings indicate that mindfulness exercises with internal focus (body scan) and external focus (mindful listening) can have positive effects com-pared to spontaneous coping on pain tolerance, pain threshold, pain un-pleasantness, frequency of negative thoughts, and belief in thought content during subsequent pain induction. Although we found large differences be-tween the two mindfulness exercises on attentional focus after training, and moderate effects on attentional focus during pain induction, no differ-ences were found between internal and external focus conditions on out-come measures.
Emotion Regulation in Pain
68
Theoretical Implications
Enhancing CBT with Mindfulness and Emotion Regulation
Our findings from Study I indicate that enhancing CBT with strategies and skills training from DBT can be an effective approach for chronic pain patients with emotional distress. Moreover, the mediation analysis in Study II strengthens this claim by showing that positive long-term effects of the hybrid treatment compared to iCBT, may indeed be related to im-proved pain-related and general emotion dysregulation. In addition, the findings from Study III align with previous claims that brief mindfulness exercises can have positive acute effects on pain tolerance, pain threshold, and pain unpleasantness (Shires et al., 2020; Zorn et al., 2020), adding that these effects can be noticeable in experimentally induced pain regardless of the attentional focus used during the exercise.
Within-group effects of the hybrid treatment at 9-month follow-up were large on symptoms of depression, general anxiety, pain catastrophiz-ing, and pain interference, with more impact on symptoms of depression and pain interference compared to the overall moderate effects of iCBT. These findings are coherent with the results of the initial feasibility study (Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014), indicating positive effects of the hybrid treat-ment on catastrophizing, acceptance, and negative affect. In addition, the moderate effects of iCBT align with previous findings showing small effects of CBT on similar outcomes among patients with chronic pain (Williams et al., 2020). Hence, it is plausible that the hybrid treatment may indeed be a more effective approach than other forms of CBT. However, within-group effect sizes should be interpreted with caution since baseline and post-treatment scores are dependent, and effects can be influenced by unknown confounders (Cuijpers et al., 2016). In other words, the hybrid treatment needs to be compared to a passive control condition to adequately estimate its non-relative effectiveness. The relative effects of the hybrid treatment compared to iCBT were moderate on pain interference at both measure points, and small on symptoms of depression and pain catastrophizing.
Our results from Study I also align with previous findings showing pos-itive effects of mindfulness-based interventions for individuals with psy-chiatric disorders (Hofmann & Gómez, 2017) and chronic pain (Veehof et al., 2016). It is, however, essential to consider the differences between these interventions in terms of treatment aims, methods, and outcomes before concluding that mindfulness-based strategies are universally effective. Sev-eral reviews emphasize the lack of coherence in results of RCT’s on mind-
fulness-based treatments, likely attributable to this heterogeneity (Cardle et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021). For instance, the hybrid treatment use emotion regulation strategies from DBT. While these are mindfulness-
Discussion
69
based, promoting acceptance, self-compassion, and metacognitive aware-ness, they place less emphasis on training attention and introspective awareness compared to other treatments such as MBSR or MBCT (Chiesa & Malinowski, 2011). Although our findings from Study III indicate that attentional focus may not be essential for acute effects on experimental pain, it remains unclear if these mechanisms have an impact in mindful-ness interventions for chronic pain. In addition, the emotion regulation training employed in the hybrid treatment entails learning previously men-tioned skills, practicing them in several contexts, and discuss different out-comes with an experienced clinical psychologist (Linton & Klein-Strand-berg, 2022). Hence, results of the hybrid treatment may not align with in-terventions focusing exclusively on mindfulness training, without this col-laborative dialogue.
In his reflections on the hybrid treatment, Lumley (2019) comment on using emotion regulation strategies from DBT, noting that they were origi-nally developed for patients with excessive emotional intensity. He sug-gested that many patients with chronic pain may instead need interven-tions encouraging experiencing and expressing emotions, due to excessive emotional avoidance and suppression. This is particularly relevant since difficulties to identify and express emotions has been associated with pain intensity and interference (Aaron et al., 2022). However, I am not certain that the hybrid treatment communicates the idea that emotions need to be controlled.
As stated in the introduction, emotion regulation is seen as a complex process that involves both expressing emotions and inhibiting dysfunc-tional responses (Gross, 2002). Moreover, the acceptance-based definition used in mindfulness-based approaches explicitly encourage willingness to experience emotions (Gratz & Tull, 2010). Therefore, I would argue that a tailored approach using skills training from DBT could effectively address both excessive emotional intensity and emotional avoidance. The training would focus on acceptance, expression, and inhibition of emotional re-sponses, depending on the context, specific needs, and desired outcomes for the patient. Indeed, an entire section of the hybrid treatment manual is dedicated to practicing emotional disclosure, i.e., sharing and expressing intimate experiences and feelings (Linton & Klein-Strandberg, 2022). It is also worth noting that the measures used to assess emotion regulation skills in these studies, such as DERS, SCS-12 and CPAQ, include several items regarding emotional awareness and acceptance of emotional experi-ences (Raes et al., 2011; Fish et al., 2010; Gratz & Roemer, 2004).
Emotion Regulation in Pain
70
Combining Emotion Regulation and Exposure Therapy
The most salient differences between the hybrid treatment and iCBT where on pain inference, suggesting that the hybrid treatment more effi-ciently altered the negative influence of pain on work, leisure activities, and socializing. Moreover, the results from Study II suggests that these im-provements were related to reduced catastrophizing, fear of movement, and increased pain acceptance. These are all processes targeted by emotion regulation training, exposure in vivo, and behavioral experiments. It is therefore plausible that these interventions were essential for treatment outcomes. Furthermore, these findings align with other studies indicating that effects of CBT on pain interference might be mediated by decreased catastrophizing and increased pain acceptance (Murillo et al., 2022).
However, the modest proportions of clinically significant improve-ments of the hybrid treatment (<30% per outcome), as well as lack of im-pact on pain intensity, indicate that there is room to further enhance the treatment. A recent evaluation of attempts to implement the hybrid treat-ment in clinical settings by Löfstrand et al. (2023), revealed that therapists less inclined to adjust treatment content questioned if the hybrid treat-ment, and specifically exposure in vivo related to fear of movements, was relevant for all patients. Indeed, it has been suggested that the fear-avoid-ance model, which underlies exposure in vivo, mainly applies to a specific subgroup of pain patients who fear that engaging in painful movements or activities could lead to further bodily harm or injuries (Vlaeyen & Crombez, 2020). However, although not all patients demonstrate these difficulties, the proportion of pain patients for whom similar interventions might be beneficial could be substantial. A recent study using a large sample of adults with chronic pain reported that approximately 46% scored high on measures related to pain-related emotion dysregulation, and only 25% re-ported skilful pain-related and general emotion regulation (Aaron et al., 2023). This aligns with findings indicating that the prevalence of fear of movements among patients with chronic pain falls between 51-72% (Bor-deleau et al., 2022). Given that the hybrid treatment combines exposure with skills training to address dysfunctional avoidance related to both pain and emotions (Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014), it is likely to be applicable and beneficial for a wide range of patients experiencing comorbid pain and emotional distress.
The concerns outlined by Löfstrand (2023), also align with previous re-search highlighting the challenges of pinpointing distinct avoidance behav-iors among chronic pain patients (Linton & Fruzzetti, 2014). As mentioned in the introduction, pain patients do not necessarily regard avoidance as unreasonable, and many do not report significant levels of catastrophizing, fear, or disability (Wideman et al., 2013). In addition, it has been suggested
Discussion
71
that therapists might be influenced by the patient’s avoidance agenda (Lin-ton & Klein-Strandberg, 2022; Vlaeyen et al., 2012). These factors can in-deed pose challenges in both recognizing the necessity for repeated expo-sure to unpleasant experiences, and in motivating the therapist and the pa-tient. As suggested by Lumley (2019), the treatment manual does explicitly suggest that exposure is complemented with information that pain can be a “false alarm”, unrelated to actual harm. In addition, it was recommended to involve a physiotherapist or medical expert to address any misconcep-tions about the potential harm of physical activities and movements. How-ever, it is plausible that these aspects of the treatment could be further re-fined, and that therapists may require more extensive training to reduce catastrophizing and fear of movements efficiently.
Regarding the suggestion to incorporate a less agnostic explanation of where pain comes from (Lumley, 2019), this would require careful consid-erations of both theoretical and ethical aspects. There are numerous factors from biological and psychosocial perspectives to consider for each individ-ual before attempting to draw conclusions on the etiology of pain (Adams & Turk, 2018; Gatchel et al., 2007; Linton et al., 2018; Walters & Williams, 2019). In addition, it is important to recognize that attributing physical symptoms to psychological factors is likely to result in the individual feeling offended, questioned, or distrusted (Stone et al., 2003). Moreover, patients could be rejected and distrusted by others if their pain is associated with explanations that are less widely accepted (Ruddere & Craig, 2016).
From another perspective, it is possible that effects of the hybrid treat-ment on pain interference may entail increased pain intensity for some pa-tients as they engage in valued activities rather than striving for pain-relief. Based on my clinical experience, behavioral experiments frequently result in the conclusion that a valued activity may entail increased pain intensity. However, patients can remain motivated to continue with these activities if they also result in positive and meaningful experiences. Indeed, our find-ings from Study I and II illustrate that the hybrid treatment, despite lack of influence on pain intensity, was more effective than iCBT on pain interfer-ence and symptoms of depression. Moreover, these effects were mediated by the impact on latent variables encompassing measures of pain avoid-ance and behavioral activation. These findings also align with hypotheses that lack of meaningful activities can be an important underlying factor of depression in chronic pain (Linton & Bergbom, 2011). In other words, it is plausible that some patients may encounter a trade-off between pain inten-sity and psychological well-being.
Overall, combining emotion regulation strategies and exposure in vivo seem to be an effective treatment approach. Furthermore, our findings in Study I regarding treatment acceptability, suggest that this method can be
Emotion Regulation in Pain
72
considered credible and satisfactory among participants. It is, however, im-portant to emphasize that the aim of Study I or II was not to establish that adding emotion regulation training would improve effects of exposure in vivo, nor that exposure in vivo after skills training would be essential to these obtain effects. To accomplish that objective, alternative research methods and control conditions should have been used. I will discuss this further in the section on methodological considerations.
Mechanisms of Mindfulness
The absence of differences on outcomes between external and internal focus in Study III, could be argued to align with suggestions that internal awareness in the context of mindfulness may be functional (Cayoun et al., 2017; de Jong et al., 2016; Shapiro et al., 2006), and not comparable to a maladaptive self-focus, or attentional bias towards pain, described in other contexts (Broadbent et al., 2022; Sharpe et al., 2010). Furthermore, the re-duced focus towards pain and a more dispersed focus towards other areas, reported in both experimental conditions, support the idea that broadening of awareness could be an important component of mindfulness interven-tions (Garland et al., 2015; Shapiro et al., 2006; Verhaeghen, 2020).
The findings from Study III could also be compared to previous studies to generate hypotheses regarding the effect of other mindfulness compo-nents on pain-related outcomes. For example, it is worth noting that Sharpe et al. (2010), using an exercise similar to mindful listening without training acceptance and metacognitive awareness, found an effect on pain threshold but not pain tolerance. Moreover, studies investigating the effect of acceptance and metacognitive awareness, without training attentional control, have found effects on pain tolerance but not pain threshold (For-syth & Hayes, 2014; Y. Wang et al., 2019). In conclusion, it is plausible that effects on pain tolerance may be more related to metacognitive processes, and effects on pain threshold to attentional control or broadening of atten-tion. However, this claim remains purely hypothetical as there have been no direct comparisons made between the suggested independent variables.
Regarding the impact of mindfulness exercises on emotion regulation, we did not find support for hypotheses that increased internal awareness have an impact on the use of acceptance or reappraisal strategies (Garland et al., 2017; Price & Weng, 2021; Roberts et al., 2021). However, the ab-sence of significant effects on mindfulness processes also aligns with pre-vious findings suggesting that noticeable changes in state mindfulness ap-pear after several days or weeks of mindfulness training (Baer et al., 2012; Basso et al., 2019; Haliwa et al., 2021). In other words, it is unsurprising that effects on self-reported use of regulation strategies are not noticeable after merely 12 minutes of training. In addition, it has been suggested that self-assessment of mindfulness skills can be problematic since training
Discussion
73
might be required to understand the questions and accurately identify and report states of mindfulness (Bergomi et al., 2012). This claim is also sup-ported by our findings, since all participants reported exceptionally hight levels of acceptance, including those with lower pain tolerance (i.e., acting on impulses to avoid discomfort). From this perspective, the lower rates of acceptance reported after mindfulness training could be interpreted as ef-fects of a more informed and valid assessment, rather than a negative im-pact on use of acceptance strategies during the CPT.
Using an Individualized and Tailored Approach
While the hybrid treatment manual emphasizes the role of the therapist in selecting interventions and customizing the treatment based on identi-fied behavioral patterns (Linton & Klein-Strandberg, 2022), the iCBT in-tervention followed a less flexible approach, providing the same treatment modules and homework assignments to all patients. It is plausible that this had an impact on outcomes, since findings from other studies indicate that tailoring treatments to patients needs and preferences can be a more effec-tive approach than using standardized protocols (Schaeuffele et al., 2021). Furthermore, tailoring treatments have been suggested to increase treat-ment credibility and have positive effects on treatment adherence and sat-isfaction (Barbosa et al., 2012). Hence, the tailored approach could explain differences between the hybrid treatment and iCBT regarding treatment acceptability and adherence.
It could also be argued that the tailored approach is supported by the findings from Study II, demonstrating that indirect effects on outcomes through pain-related emotion dysregulation was more salient among pa-tients scoring high on these measures pre-treatment. In other words, this might indicate that targeting non-acceptance, catastrophizing, and avoid-ance, may be more effective among individuals were there is a clear indica-tion that these processes need to be addressed. This is, however, a hypoth-esis that would require further investigations with control over relevant confounders. For example, an alternative interpretation of the results from Study II could be that moderated indirect effects are found because thera-pists in the hybrid treatment already tailor interventions, plausibly provid-ing more exposure and emotion regulation training for patients expressing difficulties that might be improved with these interventions.
In addition, the results from Study III might be useful, in combination with other findings and theories, for clinicians interested in tailoring treat-ments. For instance, even though we did not find that attentional focus had an impact on coping with experimentally induced pain, there are other fac-tors to consider when deciding what interventions to use in treatments. These factors include the necessity to increase awareness of problematic
Emotion Regulation in Pain
74
implicit strategies, behavioral patterns, and interoceptive experiences (Pa-risi et al., 2023), as well as indications for reducing problematic attentional biases (Broadbent et al., 2022) or a maladaptive self-focus (Watkins & Teasdale, 2004). While our preliminary findings need further validation among chronic pain patients in clinical settings, the indication that mind-fulness exercises with both internal and external attentional focus can have positive acute effects on pain tolerance, threshold, and unpleasantness in experimentally induced pain presents some insights. It can also be helpful to know that while the body scan might temporarily broaden internal awareness towards several areas of the body, this does not necessarily en-tail increased attention towards a localized pain or discomfort.
Methodological Considerations
Experimental Designs
Although experimental designs can provide evidence for causal rela-tionships by utilizing randomization and controlling for potential con-founders (Hariton & Locascio, 2018; Levine & Parkinson, 2014), it is im-portant to acknowledge that these approaches also have several limitations.
One major issue is external validity due to the controlled setting of the experiment. This applies to both laboratory settings and RCT’s, since the latter, while closer to real-world clinical settings, may have limited gener-alizability due to self-referral and strict inclusion criteria. These factors can result in altered adherence, and a study population not representative of patients in clinical practice (Mulder et al., 2018). We also emphasize in the article that since we advertised the study as a comparison of interventions for individuals “with long-lasting pain who felt stressed, depressed, or wor-ried”, the results may not be generalized to pain patients who would not identify themselves with that description. It is, however, worth noting that the population in Study I-II, although self-referred and plausibly more mo-tivated than patients in clinical practice, also reported high levels of sick-leave. In addition, the majority fulfilled criteria for anxiety or depressive disorder, and reported pain in more than one body location for many years. Moreover, the reported levels of pain intensity, pain interference and psy-chological distress were comparable to a large subgroup of pain patients with higher levels on these measures pre-treatment, and low adherence to rehabilitation in Swedish specialist care (Gerdle et al., 2019).
Regarding evidence for causal relationships between treatment content and outcomes in Study I-II, the lack of correlation between adherence and outcomes (i.e., dose-response) in both conditions can be considered as con-tradictory. However, these correlations are often inconclusive in psycho-
Discussion
75
logical therapies, with optimal doses varying between 4-26 sessions de-pending on content, settings, populations, and outcomes (Glenn et al., 2013; Robinson et al., 2020). The heterogeneity among patients could re-sult in varying responses to content and interventions provided at an early stage. Consequently, some patients may experience large improvements early on, and therefore become less motivated to continue their efforts, while others need more sessions to benefit from the treatment. In other words, the lack of a noticeable dose-response relation is less surprising when considering the possible variety of reasons for non-adherence (such as early satisfactory treatment responses and treatment dissatisfaction).
Conditions in Study I-II
As an experimental condition we wanted the hybrid treatment to be employed in accordance with the manual (i.e., tailored based on clinical case formulation). While this increases external validity, since that is how we assume the approach would be used in clinical settings, it also limits our possibilities to draw conclusions regarding the effect of the intervention due to heterogeneity among participants, therapists, and assessments. Fur-thermore, the use of therapist self-reports for fidelity checks raises con-cerns about potential reporting bias on what methods were used during therapy. This further complicates the ability to conclude if effects are at-tributable to interventions described in the hybrid treatment manual.
Regarding control conditions, blinding in non-pharmaceutical studies can be a complex endeavour (Hohenschurz-Schmidt et al., 2023). To over-come these difficulties, we used a credible iCBT treatment as a control con-dition in Study I-II and described the aim neutrally as a “comparison of two
forms of CBT”. However, adherence and reported treatment credibility was
significantly higher for the hybrid treatment. Therefore, while the portion of completed content did not relate to treatment outcomes, participant ex-pectancy effects cannot be ruled out (Laferton et al., 2018). Another prob-lem with the comparison between the hybrid treatment and iCBT are the differences between conditions regarding treatment format and duration. Hence, while we can argue that the iCBT intervention is an ethical and cred-ible comparator, it is not possible to conclude with certainty that observed effects are solely attributable to the content of the hybrid treatment. It is, however, worth noting that the analysis of Study II aid us somewhat in this endeavour by suggesting that improvements on emotion dysregulation was related to better long-term outcomes compared to iCBT.
Emotion Regulation in Pain
76
Experimental Pain Induction
Experimentally induced pain in laboratory sessions may indeed be far from experiencing pain in less controlled settings, and findings are difficult to generalize to the experience of long-lasting pain. Even though experi-mental pain may replicate distribution of clinical musculoskeletal pain, it is difficult to mirror other qualities such as affective components and pain increases during movements (Ford et al., 2020). Consequently, the method is not seen as a replication of what a pain patient would experience, but rather an estimate used to provide insights into specific pain mechanisms in a more controlled setting, avoiding the complex variety of confounders often present in chronic pain conditions (Olesen et al., 2012). Hence, to understand how these mechanisms can contribute to the experience of chronic pain, findings must be compared to other studies focusing on ef-fects of mindfulness and attentional focus among pain patients.
It has also been suggested that subtle social pressure, eye contact, and proximity of the experimenter might influence CPT pain tolerance (Roche et al., 2007). In Study III we tried to minimize this effect by using audio recordings and reducing direct interaction with the experimenter. While the study was not double blinded (i.e., the experimenter new what condi-tion they had prepared for the participant), the participant did not interact with the experimenter during CPT, training, or data collection. Hence, the risk of observer bias was probably low compared to earlier studies with less control over what was said and how instructions were given.
The range of water temperatures used in CPT typically varies between studies from 0 to 7 degrees Celsius, with higher temperatures resulting in longer pain tolerance times and lower pain intensities. Therefore, it is cru-cial to reproduce the exact temperature conditions when attempting to rep-licate earlier findings and use reliable equipment that ensures a precise constant temperature of circulating water (Mitchell et al., 2004). In our study this was assured by using state-of-the-art professional equipment, which guaranteed precise cooling tailored for laboratory environments (Julabo CD-F900, Julabo Labortechnik GmbH, Seelbach, Germany).
For safety reasons, a maximum immersion time typically ranging from 3 to 5 minutes is implemented when using the CPT. Hence, it is important to adjust the water temperature to minimize the number of participants who withdraw their hand before applying learned strategies, or maintain their hand submerged until the time limit when pain tolerance is an im-portant outcome variable (von Baeyer et al., 2005). In Study III, we main-tained a temperature of 5°C, to replicate the conditions of previous studies examining the effects of acceptance, mindfulness, and attention training on pain tolerance (Liu et al., 2013; Sharpe et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019). No-tably, we found that a substantial proportion of participants (42%) endured
Discussion
77
this temperature for more than 5 minutes. It is, however, uncertain if re-ducing the temperature could have resulted in obtaining more data on pain tolerance. The reported proportions of participants enduring until the max-imum time are similar in previous studies using lower temperatures (Hayes et al., 1999; Masedo & Esteve, 2007). Moreover, it has been suggested that using lower temperatures can entail that numbing effects appear more quickly (Masedo & Esteve, 2007).
Other methods that have been used to evaluate effects of mindfulness on experimental pain are electrical stimulation (Zeidan et al., 2010), and contact heat (Reiner et al., 2016; Zeidan et al., 2011, 2015). The CPT offers advantages when studying emotional responses since it seems to evoke higher estimates of unpleasantness compared to methods such as contact heat and electric stimulation (Rainville et al., 1992). Additionally, the other approaches have more limitations in terms of replicability and comparabil-ity across different methods and areas of application (Olesen et al., 2012).
Conditions in Study III
The mindfulness exercises used in Study III were brief, including a 5-8 minutes long introduction and 12 minutes of mindfulness training. This could explain the absence of effects on proposed mindfulness processes, since previous research has suggested that the impact on state mindfulness is noticeable only after several days or weeks of mindfulness practice (Baer et al., 2012; Basso et al., 2019; Haliwa et al., 2021). While our findings show that even brief interventions can have significant acute effects on pain out-comes, this limits our possibilities to understand the interplay between suggested components and long-term effects on relevant outcomes. Espe-cially since it has been suggested that repeated mindfulness practice might operate through different processes than brief exercises, with different ef-fects on pain-related outcomes (Chiesa et al., 2013; Gard et al., 2012; Petter et al., 2014), as well as increased use of reappraisal over time with long-term effects on positive affect (Garland, Hanley, et al., 2017). Furthermore, it has also been suggested that exercises delivered by a practitioner might be more effective than using audio recordings (McClintock et al., 2019). In conclusion, the impact of our brief audio recorded exercises may be some-what limited compared to more extensive training together with a skilled clinician. Employing brief and recorded exercises was, however, consid-ered the most feasible approach, offering control over potential confound-ers, while still having an impact on primary outcomes.
Another aspect of the mindfulness exercises to take into consideration is the training of attentional control by shifting focus between different body parts (body scan) our sounds (mindful listening). The impact of these exercises may not be generalized to other mindfulness approaches using
Emotion Regulation in Pain
78
one attentional anchor, such as sensations of breathing, or emphasizing open awareness early on during training. As mentioned in the introduction, focusing on one or more specific locations or stimuli could be essential to enhance attentional control (Verhaeghen, 2020).
Regarding the use of a scientific podcast for the spontaneous coping condition, we recognize that this does not mimic the other experimental conditions regarding credibility as an intervention. Indeed, it has been sug-gested that the effects of mindfulness on pain tolerance may be driven by placebo (Davies et al., 2021). Since we don’t have a credibility check to com-
pare the potential placebo influence of conditions, we can neither rule out nor confirm this hypothesis.
Measures
Self-Report Measures
The findings from Study I-II rely solely on self-report measures, and most outcomes in Study III except for pain tolerance, are also based on self-reports. Historically, most psychology research have used this approach, and it has provided valuable insights (Tull & Aldao, 2015). Self-report measures are often the most feasible and efficient way to gather data on subjective experiences, allowing for large sample sizes and streamlined data collection processes (Chan, 2010; Haeffel & Howard, 2010). Neverthe-less, it is important to acknowledge and address the many limitations of using self-reported outcomes such as response and memory biases, limited insight into automatic processes, lack of objective verification, and individ-ual differences in self-awareness (Bergomi et al., 2012; Bettis et al., 2018; Ciuk et al., 2015; Tan & Cole, 2019; Tull & Aldao, 2015).
The lack of more objective behavioral measures in RCT’s of psycholog-
ical treatments for chronic pain, has been described as a significant chal-lenge for the field (Morley & Williams, 2006). However, behavioral measures are not without their limitations. They often involve participants responding within highly structured situations, which can potentially in-fluence their behavior and prompt them to perform at their best. Moreover, relying solely on behavioral measures may not capture typical behaviors across a wider range of contexts. In contrast, self-report measures offer a different perspective by assessing how participants generally behave in var-ious situations. Thus, it has been recommended to incorporate both behav-ioral and self-report measures to assess outcomes (Dang et al., 2020).
The findings of study I-II could have been strengthened by also incor-porating objective performance measures, repeated independent clinician conducted structured interviews, or register data on work absence and medication use. Emotion regulation can be measured using a variety of
Discussion
79
methods including behavioral measures (facial expression, vocal tone, body language, and avoidance behaviors); physiological measures (heart rate, skin conductance, or neural activity); and multimethod approaches combining these techniques (Cisler et al., 2009; Sari et al., 2022; Seeley et al., 2015; Visted et al., 2017). In addition, other methods for pain assess-ment less reliant on verbal communication have been suggested, such as analysis of facial expressions. This is, however, still under development as many studies have failed to correlate facial expressions with subjective pain intensity ratings (Fontaine et al., 2022).
Unvalidated Measures
Another limitation worth mentioning is that some of the scales used in these studies have not undergone the rigorous process of scale develop-ment and validation. This raises concerns regarding their ability to accu-rately measure the intended construct, and provide consistent and compa-rable results with minimal measurement error. Specifically, in Study III, the attentional focus manipulation check was developed from scratch due to lack of better alternatives. Furthermore, the modified SERI question-naire, employed to evaluate the use of regulation strategies in Study III, was not subjected to validation procedures following translation and mod-ification. Additionally, we were unable to identify a comprehensive valida-tion of the Swedish translations of PASS or GAD-7 scales. This presents a concern, since alterations in wording and cultural context could potentially influence meaning and measurement properties (Boateng et al., 2018).
Various aspects of attention can be assessed through validated subjec-tive and objective measures. Subjective measures include self-reports using questionnaires regarding attentional control and our ability to perceive stimuli (Murphy et al., 2019; Reinholdt-Dunne et al., 2013). Objective measures include neuropsychological tests to test attentional function (Na-siri et al., 2023), and eye-tracking techniques to assess the focus of visual attention (Armstrong & Olatunji, 2012; Ayiei, 2020). Tests of attentional bias, such as a modified version of the dot-probe task (Dehghani et al., 2003; Sharpe et al., 2010), and the emotional stroop-task (Amaro-Díaz et al., 2022), has also been used in several studies regarding acute and chronic pain. However, we concluded that these approaches were not appropriate to evaluate attentional focus during the CPT.
To keep the experiment of Study III within a reasonable timeframe, we also utilized a set of single-item measures regarding distress, negative thoughts, belief in the content of thinking, awareness, willingness, and ac-ceptance. These measures lack established reliability and validity, and also run the risk of oversimplifying the constructs, failing to capture important
Emotion Regulation in Pain
80
nuances and variability. Moreover, single-item measures can entail an in-creased vulnerability to acquiescence bias (i.e., yea or naysaying) and re-sponse bias, since respondents may demonstrate a tendency to agree, or provide socially desirable responses to portray themselves favourably (Al-len et al., 2022). Regardless, one-dimensional pain scales are commonly employed as a simple and efficient method to assess pain intensity and other aspects of pain, such as its unpleasantness and pain-related distress (Olesen et al., 2012). Hence, we concluded that this was the best approach considering the time constraints of the experiment.
When considering the use of mindfulness-skills in experimental set-tings, there are a couple of feasible measures available. One such measure is the Toronto Mindfulness Scale (TMS) assessing state-like experiences during meditation (Lau et al., 2006). Another measure is the state version of the Cognitive Fusion Questionnaire (SCFQ), evaluating states of meta-cognitive awareness in experimental contexts (Bolderston et al., 2019). However, these measures have not been previously translated into Swe-dish. Moreover, during the preparation of Study III, pilots did not respond well to direct translations of the items in these questionnaires. As a result, we made the decision not to proceed with these alternatives. An alternative and simpler approach that had been used previously, involved assessing the believability of thoughts using a 1-item visual analog scale (Mandavia et al., 2015; Masuda et al., 2008). Hence, taking practical considerations into account, we evaluated the belief in thought content using the same 0-10 scale that was used for the one-dimensional pain measures.
Statistical Methods
Some would argue that the general linear model, which underlies par-ametric models, is inherently robust. However, it has been demonstrated that this assumption is incorrect (Field & Wilcox, 2017). Moreover, while non-parametric tests can be valuable in situations where the distributional assumption is violated, it is important to note that relying solely on non-parametric tests does not guarantee robustness, and the interpretation of results can be challenging. Instead, it is recommended to prioritize the use of robust models. Robust models exhibit greater resilience to outliers, offer more flexibility in modelling assumptions, provide more accurate estima-tions, and generally strike a better balance between robustness and effi-ciency. It is suggested that these models should always be considered in psychological research, since it is common for this data to deviate from a normal distribution. Considering the suggestions by Field & Wilcox (2017) described above, we employed robust models in all studies to assess direct and indirect effects on outcomes.
Discussion
81
Handling Missing Data
Missing data poses a significant challenge in RCT’s (Hariton & Locas-cio, 2018), and analysis procedures often struggle to address this issue ef-fectively. Methods like case or listwise deletion, commonly used in statisti-cal programs, assume that data is missing completely at random (MCAR), meaning that missing data is unrelated to any observed or unobserved var-iables. However, in randomized controlled trials of clinical interventions, it is unlikely that this assumption is correct. Fortunately, there are two rec-ommended approaches for handling missing data under the more lenient assumption that data is missing at random (MAR), in which observed var-iables in the model are allowed to be associated with missing data. The first approach is maximum likelihood (ML), which estimates the model param-eters based on the available observed data. The second approach is Bayes-ian multiple imputation (MI), which replaces missing values with plausible estimates based on observed data. Both ML and Bayesian MI provide more reliable and valid results when dealing with MAR data compared to the as-sumption of MCAR (Schafer & Graham, 2002).
In Study I-II a large proportion (82%) completed follow-up assess-ment. Moreover, all primary analytic models used full information maxi-mum likelihood (FIML) to estimate model parameters and their associated standard errors. Hence, all participants who were randomized were in-cluded in the primary outcome analysis, following the principle of inten-tion-to-treat analyses (McCoy, 2017). In addition, considering that baseline anxiety was related to the likelihood of missing data in Study I, we con-ducted a sensitivity analysis by reanalysing the data using MI. MI, as out-lined by Enders (2010), and FIML both operate under the MAR assump-tion and generally yield similar results when applied to large samples with the same set of variables. However, the MAR assumption requires that all observed variables associated with the missing data are incorporated into the analysis to ensure accurate results. Hence, as suggested by Collins et al. (2001), employing an inclusive strategy with more variables is often pref-erable to reduce bias and enhance efficiency. In Study I, the MI model uti-lized all outcome variables measured at pre-treatment.
Mediation Analysis
A major limitation of the mediation analysis in Study II is the lack of data, due to few measure points and a relatively small sample size. Alt-hough there is a time lag between mediators (assessed post-treatment) and outcomes (assessed at follow-up), it is not possible to confirm that effects on mediators come before the effects on outcomes, as effects on outcomes could have already occurred post-treatment. To establish that mediators reliably precede outcomes, more measure points should be used to provide
Emotion Regulation in Pain
82
a more accurate estimation of path coefficients (Cain et al., 2017). It is also important to emphize that, while causal relationships can be established regarding effects of treatment on mediators (a-paths), the association between mediators and outcomes (b-paths) is correlational (MacKinnon et al., 2007). Regarding sample size, we mention in the article that it is in the lower range for the use of SEM-models (Wolf et al., 2013). However, we also emphasize that the benefits of the models surpass this disadvantage.
Using Latent Variables
In Study II, we reduced the amount of overlapping observed variables to a reduced set of latent dimensions, commonly referred to as latent vari-ables (Cheung & Lau, 2015; B. Muthén & Asparouhov, 2014). By employing this approach, we were able to analyse and understand the relationships among mediators more effectively. Furthermore, it enabled us to test im-portant methodological assumptions related to longitudinal mediation analysis, such as longitudinal measurement invariance. This means that we could assess whether the measurement properties of our variables re-mained consistent over time, which is crucial for drawing reliable conclu-sions about mediation effects in longitudinal studies. In addition, the ap-proach enabled us to address issues related to measurement error, i.e., dis-crepancies between the true and observed values, which can introduce noise and bias to the analysis (McArdle, 2009). Moreover, this approach offers the advantage of reducing the number of statistical tests required for mediation analysis. This can prevent inflated type-1 error rates, which oc-cur when the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis is increased due to conducting multiple tests (Feise, 2002). The use of latent factors in SEM may also be important in mediation analyses to overcome problems asso-ciated with shared variance (Cheung & Lau, 2015; B. Muthén & As-parouhov, 2014). Indeed, our analysis in Study II indicated a substantial overlap among indicators for the latent variables. Hence, modelling them separately would have been problematic.
While the advantages of this approach are numerous, there are also some drawbacks worth mentioning. For instance, using latent variables can affect replication and the use of outcomes in meta-analyses (Ledgerwood & Shrout, 2011). The results of Study II could have contributed more to the meta-analysis by Murillo et al. (2022) by using observed variables such as pain catastrophizing. In addition, while we justify the use of latent variables by stating what aspects of emotion dysregulation they capture, it is im-portant to acknowledge that not all these measures are constructed from theories specifically related to emotion regulation. For example, BADS, while capturing situation selection, rumination, and response modulation,
Discussion
83
was developed from theories underpinning operant behavioral interven-tions. Hence, these behavioral responses are not described as emotion reg-ulation strategies, even though they could be understood as such from the theoretical framework of this thesis. Indeed, subsequent publications have used slightly different measures to assess these latent constructs (Aaron et al., 2023).
Suggestions for Future Studies To summarize the mentioned considerations and provide suggestions
for future studies, I propose the following. Studies regarding the efficacy of the hybrid treatment may consider en-
suring a representative sample of chronic pain patients by implementing and testing the treatment in various clinical settings. To evaluate the effi-cacy of the hybrid treatment, it should also be compared to treatment as usual or wait list controls. Moreover, future studies could investigate if combining exposure in vivo with emotion regulation strategies was crucial to gain improved efficacy compared to iCBT, and not some other non-spe-cific factor such as alliance or face-to-face interactions. To this end, the hy-brid treatment might be compared to an active control condition better matched in format, delivery, and content, depending on the specific hy-potheses of the study. In addition, to minimize reporting bias, and ensuring that therapist indeed followed the manual, independent judgment of video or audio recordings could be used for fidelity checks if practically feasible.
Further research is also needed to investigate causality between medi-ators and outcomes. For example, more repeated measure points could es-tablish temporal precedence of mediators, which would add more robust support to the theoretical model. Future studies using the suggested statis-tical models for moderated mediation could also consider increasing the sample size.
Even though we did not identify differences between mindfulness ex-ercises with external and internal attentional focus among healthy partici-pants, this may not apply to chronic pain patients. Especially among those with higher levels of catastrophizing, hypervigilance, or lack of internal awareness. Hence, future studies could investigate how these exercises ad-dress the specific needs of these patients. It would also be interesting to evaluate effects of manipulating other key mechanisms, such as attentional control, metacognitive awareness, and acceptance.
Finally, a general suggestion for future studies is to incorporate objec-tive performance measures, observational or physiological measures, and register data on sickness absence and healthcare-seeking behaviors, to val-idate and confirm self-reported outcomes.
Emotion Regulation in Pain
84
Conclusions
85

##### MAIN CONCLUSIONS

In accordance with the overarching aim of this thesis, our findings sug-gest that CBT could be enhanced for chronic pain patients experiencing emotional distress by incorporating emotion regulation strategies and skills training from mindfulness-based interventions.
In Study I we conclude that a tailored transdiagnostic hybrid treatment approach, integrating exposure and emotion regulation strategies from DBT, may be considered a promising and effective treatment option for these patients. The hybrid treatment was more effective than iCBT on pri-mary outcomes related to pain interference and emotional distress, at post-treatment and 9-month follow-up. Our analysis in Study II provided fur-ther support for the conceptual principles of the hybrid treatment by show-ing that positive long-term effects were mediated by improved pain-related and general emotion dysregulation. Finally, our findings in Study III sug-gest that brief mindfulness exercises, regardless of attentional focus, can have positive acute effects on pain tolerance, pain threshold, pain unpleas-antness, belief in thought content, and frequency of negative thoughts, among healthy participants experiencing experimentally induced pain.
In conclusion, integrating mindfulness-based emotion regulation strategies from DBT with exposure therapy seem to have positive long-term effects among patients with chronic pain and emotional distress, by reduc-ing pain interference with daily activities and improving psychological well-being. However, the relatively modest proportions of clinically signif-icant improvements in Study I suggest that there might be room to further enhance the hybrid treatment. This ignited the curiosity to explore moder-ated mediation of treatment effects in Study II and delve deeper into the impact of specific mechanisms of mindfulness in Study III. As argued in the discussion, the hybrid treatment could, in theory, be useful for a large proportion of patients with pain and emotional distress, since the treat-ment target avoidance of both pain and emotional responses. In addition, skills training from DBT, and other mindfulness-based approaches, en-compass a large range of emotion regulation strategies, encouraging both expressing emotions and inhibiting dysfunctional responses. Hence, the treatment could potentially be tailored in accordance with a multitude of desired outcomes and specific contexts.
While our results align with other studies indicating that mindfulness-based interventions can be effective for patients with chronic pain and emotional disorders, there are also important differences between mind-fulness-based approaches to consider. For instance, although the hybrid
Emotion Regulation in Pain
86
treatment integrates exposure with mindfulness skills such as acceptance, self-compassion, and metacognitive awareness, less emphasis is put on training mindful awareness and attentional control. Instead, more effort is invested in discovering and practicing functional regulation skills in differ-ent contexts by collaborating with an experienced therapist. Little is known, however, about the impact of these specific mindfulness skills and treatment mechanisms. While some studies indicate that metacognitive awareness, acceptance, and attentional control may be important factors, the impact of attentional deployment remains unclear. Indeed, our findings from Study III indicate that attentional focus may not be essential to achieve positive acute effects of mindfulness on pain behaviors and experi-ences, at least among healthy participants coping with experimentally in-duced pain.
Although it remains inconclusive how the hybrid treatment can be fur-ther improved, our findings provide some insights for future research re-garding the importance of targeting pain-related dysregulation, and possi-bilities of using mindfulness exercises with different attentional focus. Hopefully, this might pave the way for further exploration and experimen-tation on transdiagnostic treatments for individuals with chronic pain and emotional distress.
